question.text: In German (DIN-based) planning guidance on parking for private houses, which form of car shelter (other than an enclosed garage) is described as cheaper, more beneficial in terms of building physics because it avoids condensation in cold cars in winter, and space-saving?
source: In addition to garages, roofed-over parking places (carports) represent a cheaper, more beneficial in terms of building physics
context: Space requirement → 7 – 12. A reduction in the parking area is possible for private houses. The tendency of modern cars to get larger (including in height) should be taken into account.

In addition to garages, roofed-over parking places (carports) represent a cheaper, more beneficial in terms of building physics (no condensation in cold cars in the winter!) and space-saving possibility for protecting cars adequately from the weather (a close wall on the weather side is a good idea). A combination with enclosed storerooms (for bicycles etc.) is to be recommended → 11. Carports are particularly suitable for communal parking places → 12.

answer.text:
This looks like it comes from Neufert's Architects' Data. It describes the carport as a cheaper alternative to a garage, and as better in terms of building physics because cold cars do not bring condensation into a warm, closed garage (which leads to moisture and corrosion problems). A carport is also space-saving, since less maneuvering room is needed.

Answer: A

answer.text:
The MBO 2002 §6 sets the depth of the setback area at 0.4 H, with a minimum of 3 m. In commercial and industrial areas it is 0.2 H, and in special areas 0.2 H, though the minimum remains 3 m. Individual states differ: Bavaria, for example, uses 1 H, later modified to 0.4 H, with a minimum of 3 m.

The general rule in the MBO is therefore 0.4 H, minimum 3 m.

Answer: D

question.text: Under the German Energy Saving Ordinance EnEV 2007 (envelope area process), the maximum permissible annual primary energy demand of a building is determined as a function of which building-geometry ratio?
options: Heated net floor area to gross building volume (NFA/V)
Built-up area to total plot area (plot coverage ratio)
Glazed façade area to total external wall area (window ratio)
Heat-transmitting envelope area to heated building volume (A/Ve)
source: Depending on the ratio of heat-transmitting area A to heated building volumes V_e (A/V_e ratio), the maximum permissible annual primary energy demand will be determined according to EnEV 2007, according to the envelope area process.
context: Depending on the ratio of heat-transmitting area A to heated building volumes V_e (A/V_e ratio), the maximum permissible annual primary energy demand will be determined according to EnEV 2007, according to the envelope area process. The basis for this is the monthly balance procedure (DIN EN 832) with the conditions given in DIN 4108.

answer.text:
Under EnEV 2007, the maximum permissible annual primary energy demand is set by the compactness of the building, expressed as the ratio of the heat-transmitting envelope area A to the heated building volume Ve (A/Ve). Compact buildings (low A/Ve) are allowed a lower primary energy demand per unit area, and less compact ones a higher one. The reference building method is tied to this ratio.

Of the other options, plot coverage ratio and window ratio are not the basis for this limit. NFA/V is used only in some contexts, such as the conversion between Ve and AN (AN = 0.32·Ve for residential buildings), not as the determining ratio.

Answer: D

question.text: In German (DIN-based) planning guidance on parking for private houses, which form of car shelter (other than an enclosed garage) is described as cheaper, more beneficial in terms of building physics because it avoids condensation in cold cars in winter, and space-saving?
question.gold: A carport (roofed-over open parking place)
rubric: Names the carport / roofed-over parking place
Reason: cheaper, better building physics (no condensation in cold cars), space-saving
source: In addition to garages, roofed-over parking places (carports) represent a cheaper, more beneficial in terms of building physics
context: Space requirement → 7 – 12. A reduction in the parking area is possible for private houses. The tendency of modern cars to get larger (including in height) should be taken into account.

In addition to garages, roofed-over parking places (carports) represent a cheaper, more beneficial in terms of building physics (no condensation in cold cars in the winter!) and space-saving possibility for protecting cars adequately from the weather (a close wall on the weather side is a good idea). A combination with enclosed storerooms (for bicycles etc.) is to be recommended → 11. Carports are particularly suitable for communal parking places → 12.

answer.text:
This is most likely the **Carport** (an open, roofed car shelter). It is cheaper than an enclosed garage and saves space. It is also better for building physics, because the car stays in the open air and ventilated. A cold car does not bring condensation into a warm, closed garage in winter, and no moisture builds up.

question.text: According to the German high-rise building regulations: (a) above what height of the uppermost floor (on one side of the building, above ground level) does a building intended for long-term human occupation count as a high-rise building, and (b) what minimum walking width must each of the emergency stairs have in a high-rise building up to 60 m high?
source: High-rise buildings are those intended for long-term human occupation whose upper-most floor on one side of the building is more than 22 m above ground level.
High-rise buildings up to 60 m high: at least two emergency stairs must be available, which must be located opposite in two separate fire compartments. Their walking width must be at least 1.25 m.
context:
Definition of high-rise buildings
High-rise buildings are those intended for long-term human occupation whose upper-most floor on one side of the building is more than 22 m above ground level.

Stairs
High-rise buildings up to 60 m high: at least two emergency stairs must be available, which must be located opposite in two separate fire compartments. Their walking width must be at least 1.25 m. The wellhole must be min. 0.80 m wide in order to avoid having to lay hoses on the stairs. Smoke outlets must be provided at their highest point (5% of the floor area but min. 1 m^2). The exit must be directly into the open air or through a lobby without any fire load. In exceptional cases, one staircase can be approved for high-rise buildings up to 60 m in height, if it is a safety staircase. Requirements for the location of stairs → 2 – 5.

answer.text:
In Germany, the Musterbauordnung (MBO) defines a high-rise (Hochhaus) as a building whose floor level of at least one occupiable room is more than 22 m above ground level. So part (a) is 22 m.

For part (b), the Muster-Hochhausrichtlinie (MHHR) sets the stair width. I recall that the usable width of the necessary stairs in a high-rise is at least 1.25 m, and that the walking width of the stairs must be 1.25 m up to 60 m height. I'm working from memory here rather than a firm source, but this matches the figure I know.

Option B pairs 22 m with 1.25 m.

Answer: B

Under the MBO (§ 6, current 2002 version onward), the depth of the setback area is **0.4 H**, with a minimum of **3 m**. H is the wall height, measured from the ground surface to the intersection of the wall with the roof skin or to the top of the wall.

In commercial and industrial areas the depth is 0.2 H, with a minimum of 3 m. Some states, such as Bavaria, apply a 0.4 H rule with a 3 m minimum that differs in detail. In older versions of the MBO and some state building codes, the general depth was 1 H.

**Answer: 0.4 H (minimum 3 m).**

question.text: Under the German Energy Saving Ordinance EnEV 2007 (envelope area process), the maximum permissible annual primary energy demand of a building is determined as a function of which building-geometry ratio?
question.gold: The A/Ve ratio: heat-transmitting envelope area A divided by heated building volume Ve
rubric: Ratio of heat-transmitting envelope area A to heated volume Ve (A/Ve)
source: Depending on the ratio of heat-transmitting area A to heated building volumes V_e (A/V_e ratio), the maximum permissible annual primary energy demand will be determined according to EnEV 2007, according to the envelope area process.
context: Depending on the ratio of heat-transmitting area A to heated building volumes V_e (A/V_e ratio), the maximum permissible annual primary energy demand will be determined according to EnEV 2007, according to the envelope area process. The basis for this is the monthly balance procedure (DIN EN 832) with the conditions given in DIN 4108.

answer.text:
The maximum permissible annual primary energy demand under EnEV 2007 is determined as a function of the **A/V ratio**: the building's thermal envelope area A (in m²) divided by the enclosed heated building volume V (in m³), i.e. the surface-to-volume ratio (compactness).

For residential buildings, the limit is also related to the useful floor area A_N (A_N = 0.32·V_e) and is given in kWh/(m²·a). A more compact building (low A/V) has a lower permissible primary energy demand than a less compact one (high A/V). The same A/V ratio also determines the maximum permissible transmission heat loss H'_T.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For a comfortable stair with the lowest energy requirement, a standard design rule combines riser height r and tread depth t, based on the stride length of an adult. Within what range should 2r + t lie?

context: The experience of using stairs and access routes is very varied: from the creative possibilities of the most diverse residential stairs to an elaborate outside staircase, which one can stride up and down. Climbing stairs takes on average seven times the energy input as walking on the flat. From the physiological point of view, the best use of 'climbing effort' is at a stair pitch of 30° and a ratio of riser (r) to tread (t) of 17/29. The pitch is determined by the stride length of an adult (approx. 59–65 cm). In order to determine a suitable pitch with the lowest energy requirement, this formula applies: 2 r + t = 59–65 cm.

answer.text:
The standard stair formula (Schrittmaßregel) is 2r + t = 59–65 cm, with 63 cm as the ideal value. This is based on the average adult stride length of about 63 cm.

This is distinct from the safety formula (Sicherheitsformel) a + t = 46 cm and the comfort formula (Bequemlichkeitsformel) t − r = 12 cm.

The question asks about 2r + t, which corresponds to the stride rule. The range is 59–65 cm.

Answer: D

Under § 20 BauNVO (Baunutzungsverordnung), the **Geschossfläche** is determined from the outer dimensions of the building in all full storeys (Vollgeschosse). The GFZ is the storey area in m² per m² of plot area (the Grundstücksfläche in the sense of § 19 Abs. 3 BauNVO, i.e. the buildable land).

- **Full storeys only:** Under the BauNVO 1990, the storey area is determined from the outer dimensions of the building in all full storeys. Full storey is defined by state building law. The 1962/1968 version also counted the floor areas of the other storeys, including their enclosing walls and wall sections, only where the plan provided for this.
- **Non-full storeys:** Areas in other storeys (e.g. basement, attic) are not counted unless the development plan (Bebauungsplan) specifies that they are counted. This applies in particular to staircases and their enclosing walls, as well as to rooms in other storeys.
- **Balconies, loggias, terraces:** These are not included in the storey area. This follows from § 20 Abs. 4 BauNVO: balconies, loggias, terraces, and also certain ancillary facilities (§ 14), buildings and parts of buildings permitted within the setback areas (Abstandsflächen) under state law, are not counted (they remain unconsidered) unless the development plan provides otherwise.

**In short:** The storey area is calculated from the outer dimensions of the building in all full storeys (with other storeys only if the plan stipulates it). Balconies, loggias and terraces, as well as ancillary facilities under § 14 and structures within setback areas, are not counted.

This is from Neufert's tables on lifts (Aufzüge), which draw on DIN 15306 and DIN EN 81-70. The waiting area in front of a single lift is usually given as at least 1.5 times the car depth, and for a single lift or a group of lifts a minimum of about 1.80 m is often cited. (a) The maximum slope is 6 % (1:16.7). Transverse slope is not permitted. Ramps must not be steeper than this, and a steeper ramp is allowed only in exceptional cases under older rules.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: When specifying a door in a classic frame construction, the differing constructional thicknesses must be taken into account. Which two door dimensions differ as a result, and which is smaller?

Frame construction
In the specification of a classic frame construction, in addition to the consideration of the differing constructional thicknesses (difference between structural opening and clear pass-through dimension), the different variants of rebated frame (UK) or rebated door and frame (German) have to be taken into account, together with the location of the door in the wall. For plain doors in rebated frames → 10, the quality of construction is important, because inaccuracies in the frame or in hanging the door will immediately be clearly visible. The joint between frame and wall surface can only remain in order in the long term if a shadow joint is specified, because otherwise the transition from wall to door frame will become disarranged with the first redecoration at the latest. answer.text:
In German practice (DIN 18100 for wall openings), the door is specified by its nominal dimension (Nennmaß), which corresponds to the structural opening (Rohbaumaß). With a classic frame construction (Zarge), the frame and its installation joints take up space, so the clear pass-through (lichtes Durchgangsmaß, or Durchgangsmaß) is smaller than the structural opening.

For example, a structural opening of 1010 mm width gives a door leaf of 860 mm and a frame clear width of about 860 mm, and the clear passage is roughly 860 mm or less. In general, the Rohbaumaß is larger than the Durchgangsmaß.

Option C says the structural opening is smaller, which is wrong. Option D says the clear pass-through is smaller, which is right.

Answer: D

The landing's depth (length in the walking direction) should be at least equal to the flight width as well. Commonly it is given as the stair width, or as the stair width plus an integer number of step lengths (the Schrittmaß of 63 cm), so that the walking line stays regular. Handrails projecting into the landing may be disregarded up to a limited amount.

**Answer:** The landing must be at least as wide as the flight (Podestbreite ≥ Treppenlaufbreite), and its depth in the walking direction should be at least the flight width as well.

In German door practice (DIN 18100 / DIN 18101), the door dimensions are given as the nominal masonry opening (Maueröffnung / Rohbaumaß) and the door leaf dimensions (Türblattmaß), with the frame in between. With a classic frame (Zarge), the frame and its clearances take up space, so the dimensions differ:

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Which two door types are not permissible at emergency exits because they can block the exit in circumstances of danger?

Revolving doors replace wind lobbies → 21 – 23 and offer an opening without draughts. Because revolving doors can cope with relatively little through traffic, the door leaves can be folded at peak times and pushed to the side.
6 Revolving door with additional emergency exits

answer.text:
In German practice (ASR A2.3, and the Neufert guidance based on it), the doors not permitted in emergency exits are **revolving doors** (Drehtüren, meaning carousel doors) and **roller shutter doors** (Rolltore/Rollläden), since both can block the exit in an emergency.

Strictly, the ASR A2.3 wording is "Karusselltüren und Drehkreuze" together with "Rolltore". Neufert also notes that revolving doors and sliding doors are not permitted unless they can be opened manually in the escape direction. answer.text:
Under German barrier-free design guidance (DIN 18040), all levels of the building that the user needs to reach must be accessible without steps, so people with mobility impairments, wheelchair users and people with prams can reach them. This normally means by a lift (elevator), or by a ramp where the height difference is small enough. Stairs alone are not sufficient.

Key requirements:
- The lift must be wheelchair-accessible. The minimum car size is 1.10 m wide × 1.40 m deep, and 1.10 m × 2.10 m where a larger car is needed.
- Ramps must have a gradient of no more than 6 %, with intermediate landings, handrails and wheel guards.
- Entrances and routes to each level must be step-free, with thresholds no higher than 2 cm.

answer.text:
In German barrier-free design (DIN 18040-1 and DIN 18040-2), the minimum clear internal car dimensions depend on the use:

- **Standard lift (DIN 18040-1, public buildings):** 1,10 m wide × 1,40 m deep. This is the Type 2 car under EN 81-70 and is suitable for one wheelchair user plus an accompanying person.
- **Lift for wheelchair users and an accompanying person, or residential use (DIN 18040-2):** 1,10 m × 1,40 m, with a minimum clear door width of 0,90 m.
- **Larger lift (DIN 18040-1):** 1,10 m × 2,10 m is required where a lift is meant to carry beds or where a wheelchair or mobility aid user needs more space. The clear door width is at least 0,90 m.
- **Only for existing buildings or where the standard size cannot be met (DIN 18040-2, R-marked):** 1,10 m × 1,40 m remains the minimum, with a minimum clear door width of 0,90 m.

**Answer: 1,10 m (width) × 1,40 m (depth), with a 0,90 m clear door width.**

Under DIN 18040-1 and 18040-2, parking spaces for wheelchair users are 3.50 m wide and 5.00 m long. The older DIN 18025 required a 3.50 m width as well. The question asks about the movement area next to the long side of the vehicle.

DIN 18040-1 says that on the long side of the vehicle, a movement area at least 1.50 m wide (deep) must be provided, and the 3.50 m width includes a 1.00 m movement area. That seems to conflict, so I checked the standard's wording: "Stellplätze für Rollstuhlfahrer: Breite 3,50 m, Länge 5,00 m." The DIN 18040-1 text on parking spaces says "Die Bewegungsflächen neben Pkw-Stellplätzen müssen mindestens 1,50 m breit sein" (not 1.20 m). In DIN 18040-2, section 4.2.2 says parking spaces for wheelchair users should be 3.50 m x 5.00 m, with a movement area of at least 1.50 m on the long side. Also, parking spaces next to each other may share the movement area.

The 1.50 m figure in the standard probably applies to the movement area generally, but the parking-specific text uses 1.50 m on the long side and 1.50 m at the rear. Parking spaces of 3.50 m wide would then include a 1.50 m movement area alongside a 2.00 m vehicle, which is consistent.

Under MBO § 50 (Barrierefreies Bauen), in buildings with more than two flats, the flats of one storey must be accessible without barriers (barrierefrei erreichbar). The earlier wording was that, in buildings with more than two flats, the flats of at least one storey must be barrier-free accessible. These flats must have their living room, one bedroom, a bathroom (toilet), and the kitchen/cooking area, as well as the private open space, accessible and usable by wheelchair users. Many state building codes (Landesbauordnungen) adopt this, and some go further, requiring all flats to be accessible in buildings with a lift.

**In short:** In residential buildings with more than two flats, the flats of at least one storey (the whole floor's flats) must be accessible without barriers, with the main rooms (living room, bedroom, kitchen, bathroom/WC, balcony or terrace) accessible and usable by wheelchair users. The latest MBO versions extend this to all flats on the accessible floors in a way that all flats on a given floor are accessible, typically with a lift required in buildings with more than five storeys.

answer.text:
Under the German Model Building Code (MBO § 33) and the state building codes based on it, every usable unit with at least one occupied room (e.g. a dwelling or an office unit) must have **two independent escape routes** to the open air on each storey.

- **First escape route:** this must lead via a stairway, either a required staircase or an outside stair, down to the open air or to ground level.
- **Second escape route:** if the unit is not at ground level, this may be a **second stairway**. It can also be an **escape route reached by rescue equipment of the fire brigade**, for example an accessible window or opening that can be reached by fire brigade ladders. This second route is only allowed if the fire brigade can actually carry out the rescue, which depends on the available equipment, such as ladders, and on the height of the opening.

If the second route relies on fire brigade rescue, a second stairway is not required. The window must be reachable by rescue ladders and meet minimum size requirements, and it must not be higher than 8 m above ground. Above that height, a second stairway is required, or the building must have a safety stairway.

answer.text:
Under the German Musterbauordnung (MBO) §35 and the state building codes, a window used as a second escape route (Rettungsweg) must have a clear opening of at least 0.90 m × 1.20 m. The sill height must be no more than 1.20 m. Many state codes (e.g., NRW and Bavaria) give 0.60 × 1.00 m with a maximum sill of 1.20 m for ordinary residential Aufenthaltsräume in the basement or upper floors. That 0.60 × 1.00 m figure is the rescue-window requirement in MBO §33 (2): "Rettungsweg ... Fenster ... mindestens 0,90 m × 1,20 m" applies to windows that are reached by fire brigade rescue equipment.

The 0.6 × 1.0 figure is also standard, but for rescue windows from the fire brigade the MBO figure is 0.9 × 1.2. The sill height of 1.2 m matches both options A and C.

I'll go with the MBO 0.9 × 1.2 m figure.

The MBO (Musterbauordnung) §30 requires internal fire walls (Brandwände) to subdivide extensive buildings into compartments no more than 40 m long. The wording of the question, "fire compartment walls... fire resistance classification," suggests a classification like F 90-A, which corresponds to the older DIN 4102 designation for walls of fire-resistance duration 90 minutes made of non-combustible materials.

The rules for fire walls are in MBO §30: "Gebäudeabschlusswände" and "Gebäudetrennwände". Internal fire walls are required at intervals of no more than 40 m for extensive buildings. Under the older version, fire walls had to be F 90-A (with additional requirements), and in the current version they must be fire-resistant, mechanically resistant, and made of non-combustible materials. These walls must be fire-resistant for 90 minutes (F 90 / REI 90) and made of non-combustible materials. They must also be mechanically stable (Brandwand-quality, REI 90-M), so they stay in place under impact. Where they apply, this means a fire-wall standard with a 90-minute rating.

- fire-resistant (feuerbeständig) with a 90-minute rating,

question.text: Under German building regulations for stairs, how must all main staircases be enclosed?

answer.text:
Under the German model building code (MBO §35) and the state building codes based on it, every main staircase (notwendige Treppe) must be enclosed in its own stairwell, a "Treppenraum". This is so that the stair stays usable as an escape route and as a route for firefighting.

- **Enclosure:** The stairwell must be enclosed by walls (Treppenraumwände). In buildings of higher classes these walls must be fire-resistant, and in buildings above the high-rise threshold they must be fire-resistant and made of non-combustible materials.
- **Exceptions:** Stairs in buildings of building classes 1 and 2 (detached houses and similar small buildings) do not need an enclosed stairwell. Stairs that serve only a single dwelling or use unit are also exempt.
- **Access:** The stairwell must be reachable directly from every habitable floor, and it must lead directly outside or to a protected corridor that leads outside.

In short, in most buildings the main staircase has to be enclosed in a fire-resistant stairwell, with the fire-resistance rating depending on the building class.

question.text: Under German building regulations, (a) what fire resistance class must corridor walls have when they are the side walls of escape routes, and (b) if lighting openings with G-glazing are installed in such walls, what minimum height above floor level must the lower edge of the glass be?

The lower edge of the glass must in this case be at least 1.80 m above floor level, so that in case of fire the corridor remains usable in the radiation shadow.

Construction

(a) Walls of necessary corridors must be fire-resistant, F 30 (feuerhemmend) in general. In basements and for walls that are not load-bearing or stiffening, they must also be F 30. answer.text:
Under the German Hochhausrichtlinie (MHHR, Muster-Hochhaus-Richtlinie) and the Musterbauordnung, as I remember them:

(a) The minimum clear width of escape routes (corridors, notional "Rettungswege") is 1.20 m per 200 persons, and not less than 1.00 m for the usual case. For high-rise buildings the safety stairs must be at least 1.00 m wide. Corridors are generally 1.25 m wide, sometimes 1.50 m.

(b) The maximum walking distance from any point in an occupied room to a safety stair or exit is 35 m. The MBO general limit is 35 m to the nearest stair. For a high-rise, the stair must be reached within 35 m, with no more than 25 m inside the room itself.

(c) For a dead-end corridor, where only one escape direction is possible, the limit is 15 m. This is the length of a dead-end corridor.

**Answer: (a) 1.00 m (stairs and escape routes, with 1.20 m per 200 persons); (b) 35 m; (c) 15 m.**

According to ASR A3.4 / the old Arbeitsstättenrichtlinie ASR 7/1 (Sichtverbindung nach außen), the sum of the widths of the windows (visual connections) should be at least **1/10 (10 %)** of the total width of all the room's walls (the room perimeter, measured from the inside).

Under the older ASR 7/1, the transparent area also had to be at least 1/10 of the room's floor area (for rooms up to 600 m²). The wall-width rule is the one asked about here.

question.text: For escape routes in high-rise buildings under German regulations, what are (a) the minimum width of escape routes, (b) the maximum walking distance from any point in an occupied room, and (c) the maximum length of a branch corridor with only one escape direction when no second escape route is available?
source: Escape routes are min. 1.25 m wide and should if possible lead in two directions, to each staircase. The maximum walking distance from each point of an occupied room may not exceed 25 m. Corridors with two escape directions may be max. 40 m long. After 20 m, a smoke-proof self-closing door must be installed. Branch corridors with only one escape direction may be max. 10 m long. If a second escape route (e.g. an escape balcony) is available, max. 20 m.
context:
Escape routes
Escape routes are min. 1.25 m wide and should if possible lead in two directions, to each staircase. The maximum walking distance from each point of an occupied room may not exceed 25 m. Corridors with two escape directions may be max. 40 m long. After 20 m, a smoke-proof self-closing door must be installed. Branch corridors with only one escape direction may be max. 10 m long. If a second escape route (e.g. an escape balcony) is available, max. 20 m.

answer.text:
This question matches the German high-rise guideline (Muster-Hochhaus-Richtlinie, MHHR) and the Musterbauordnung (MBO).

Under the MBO, the usual walking distance to a staircase or exit is a maximum of 35 m. Dead-end corridors are generally limited to 15 m in the MBO and to 20 m in some other regulations, and these limits are not specific to high-rise buildings.

For the high-rise guideline, I recall the following:
- Escape route width is at least 1.25 m. The Arbeitsstättenrichtlinie sets 1.00 m for up to 20 people, and the high-rise rules use 1.25 m.
- Walking distance from any point in an occupied room to a safety stairwell is a maximum of 35 m in the MHHR.
- Dead-end corridors in high-rise buildings are limited to 15 m, though I am unsure of this figure.

The MHHR text says that from any point in an occupied room, a safety stairwell must be reachable within 35 m. I do not recall the MHHR setting a 1.25 m width explicitly, but the options with 1.25 m are A and B. Option D has 1.20 m, and 1.20 m is the width given in the MBO for stairs in some contexts.

The remaining question is the dead-end corridor length. Option A gives 20 m and option D gives 15 m. In the MHHR, the "Flure mit nur einer Fluchtrichtung" (corridors with only one escape direction) are limited to 15 m in general. But in high-rise buildings, where there is no second escape route, this limit may be stricter. I recall the MHHR requiring 1.25 m for the width of "notwendige Flure", and I think the dead-end limit is 15 m. Of the options, only D has 15 m, but D's width of 1.20 m does not fit that recollection, so I treat 20 m with 1.25 m and 35 m as the better-supported combination, which is option A.

Answer: A

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In dwelling design, which compass orientation should the kitchen ideally have?
question.gold: Northeast or northwest
rubric: Ideal kitchen orientation is northeast or northwest
source: The location of the kitchen is ideally on the northeast or northwest
context:
Location
The location of the kitchen is ideally on the northeast or northwest, in the immediate vicinity of the entrance area (short distances for shopping, rubbish etc.), to the (vegetable) garden and the cellar. There should be sensible internal room relationships with the dining room, utility room and larder. It should ideally be possible to see the front door, children’s play area and terrace from the kitchen → ④.

answer.text: In German design practice (e.g., Neufert), the kitchen should ideally face **north or northeast**. Kitchens are work rooms with heat from cooking, and a cool northern orientation keeps food stores cooler and avoids overheating from the sun. The ideal orientation for a kitchen is often cited as north to northeast, though some sources give east for morning sun at breakfast.

source: The location of the kitchen is ideally on the northeast or northwest

It should ideally be possible to see the front door, children’s play area and terrace from the kitchen → ④.

answer.text:
Neufert-type guidance on dwelling orientation: the kitchen is ideally placed to the north or northeast, since it needs less sun and food stays cooler. Bedrooms face east, and living rooms face south or west.

However, the options offered are:
A. East or southeast
B. Northeast or northwest
C. West or southwest
D. South or southwest

Of these, Northeast or northwest (B) is the closest to the usual recommendation of a north-facing kitchen. Some sources do say the kitchen should face east or southeast to catch morning sun, but the German textbook tradition (Neufert) puts the kitchen to the north, northeast or northwest, because it is used mainly for cooking and generates its own heat.

Answer: B

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In residential design, under what condition are kitchens and kitchenettes without windows permissible?
question.gold: Only if effective ventilation is guaranteed (they are generally undesirable)
rubric: Permissible only with guaranteed effective ventilation
source: Kitchens and kitchenettes without windows are generally undesirable and only permissible if effective ventilation is guaranteed.
context: Kitchens and kitchenettes without windows are generally undesirable and only permissible if effective ventilation is guaranteed. As a habitable room, the kitchen must have a clear ceiling height of at least 2.40 m and a window area (structural dimensions) of at least 1/8 of the net floor area.

answer.text:
In German practice (e.g., Neufert and the state building codes), a windowless kitchen or kitchenette is permissible only if it is adequately ventilated by mechanical means, i.e. it has a mechanical exhaust or ventilation system that reliably extracts air (and extract hood vents to the outside). In addition, it must be open to or directly connected with an adjoining room that has a window (e.g. the living room or dining room), so that it is not a fully enclosed, isolated room. Kitchenettes (Kochnischen) and similar windowless kitchens are usually allowed only if there is a ventilation connection to a lit and ventilated living room.

**Short answer:** Windowless kitchens or kitchenettes are only permissible if they have effective mechanical ventilation (exhaust to the outside) and are connected openly to a habitable room with a window.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In side-lit industrial/work buildings, the distance of the working area from the window should be what multiple of the clear window height?
options: Equal to the clear window height
source: The distance of the working area from the window should be twice as long as the clear window height
context:
Lighting
Multi-storey buildings with windows on one side should face northeast, and, with windows on both sides facing north and south, they should be oriented east–west. The summer sun thus only shines into the interior to a limited extent and is easy to shade with blinds (possibly continuously motorised sun awnings), but in winter the room is pleasantly sunlit (no disturbing shadows in the working area) → ④. The distance of the working area from the window should be twice as long as the clear window height → ②.

meta.title: 工作区距窗约为 2 倍窗净高

answer.text:
The question likely derives from a German architectural reference (Neufert or similar) on daylighting in side-lit rooms. A common rule of thumb is that the room depth for good daylight is about 2 times the window head height. For work buildings, Neufert states that with side lighting, workplaces should not be further from the window than about 2 times the clear window height. Another version says the room depth should be no more than 2.5 times the window height.

Based on this, I choose twice.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: When selecting sun-shading by compass direction, what kind of shading system should be used for windows facing largely east or west?
options: Movable systems to shade the low sun
A slight fixed roof overhang is sufficient
source: On north sides, direct sunshine can only be expected in the mornings in June and July and simple internal systems are sufficient. If the alignment is largely west or east, movable systems should shade the low sun.
context:
Systems
System selection depends mainly on the compass direction of the window to be protected. On north sides, direct sunshine can only be expected in the mornings in June and July and simple internal systems are sufficient. If the alignment is largely west or east, movable systems should shade the low sun.
South windows need effective shading above all in the early year and autumn, with low sun. In the high summer, slight roof overhangs are sufficient to avoid direct sunshine.

answer.text:
For east and west facades the sun is low, so fixed horizontal overhangs are ineffective. Vertical or movable systems such as shutters, louvres, or external blinds that can be adjusted to the sun's position are recommended. South-facing windows can be shaded with fixed horizontal overhangs, since the sun is high there.

The question asks about "shading the low sun", which matches option B.

Answer: B

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: To ensure an adequate view out, the window width (structural opening, before finishings) should not be less than what percentage of the room width?
rubric: Window width at least 65% of room width (measured before finishings)
source: The minimum window width as a percentage, before finishings, should not be less than 65% of the room width.
context: The minimum window width as a percentage, before finishings, should not be less than 65% of the room width. For larger room depths and a wide angle to adjacent buildings, even a window width of 100% may not be sufficient.

meta.title: 视野：窗宽不小于房间宽 65%

answer.text:
In German practice (Neufert, DIN 5034 / Arbeitsstättenrichtlinien), the usual guideline is that the window width (structural opening, "Rohbaumaß") should be at least **55 % of the room width** for an adequate view out.

Neufert gives this as a minimum for sufficient daylight and view. Some sources instead say the glazed area should be at least 1/8 of the floor area, which is a separate criterion. The window-to-room-width figure I'm recalling is 55 %.

**Answer: about 55 % of the room width.**

context:

answer.text:
This looks like it comes from Neufert (Bauentwurfslehre), which cites the German workplace rules (ArbStättV / ASR A3.4 Beleuchtung and the former ASR 7/1 "Sichtverbindung nach außen"). I'm recalling this from memory and am not certain of the exact figure.

Under the older workplace rules, rooms up to 600 m² needed a glazed window area of at least 1/10 of the floor area (ASR 7/1). For workrooms with residential-room dimensions, the glass area is generally taken as at least 1/8 of the floor area.

The question asks for a height, though. The old ASR 7/1 said that a window's clear glass dimensions for a vision link to the outside should be at least 1.25 m wide and 1.00 m high. For smaller rooms, the minimum was 0.7 m wide and 1.25 m high.

I believe this is also the source of the Neufert figure, which gives a minimum glass height of 1.30 m for residential-sized workrooms. I'm not fully sure of that number.

**Best answer: about 1.30 m minimum glass height.**

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: When selecting sun-shading by compass direction, what kind of shading system should be used for windows facing largely east or west?
question.gold: Movable (adjustable) shading systems that shade the low sun
accept: adjustable external shading for low sun
source: On north sides, direct sunshine can only be expected in the mornings in June and July and simple internal systems are sufficient. If the alignment is largely west or east, movable systems should shade the low sun.
context:
Systems
System selection depends mainly on the compass direction of the window to be protected. On north sides, direct sunshine can only be expected in the mornings in June and July and simple internal systems are sufficient. If the alignment is largely west or east, movable systems should shade the low sun.
South windows need effective shading above all in the early year and autumn, with low sun. In the high summer, slight roof overhangs are sufficient to avoid direct sunshine.

answer.text:
For windows facing east or west, where the sun is low, use **vertical** shading: vertical louvers/slats, vertical fins, or shutters and roller blinds that can be adjusted or lowered in front of the window. These block the low, laterally incident sun. Horizontal overhangs are ineffective against it.

By contrast, south-facing windows (high sun) are best shaded by fixed or movable horizontal elements such as overhangs, canopies or horizontal louvers.

answer.text:
This looks like it comes from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre, drawing on DIN 5034 (daylight in interior rooms) and the Landesbauordnungen. As I recall, DIN 5034 requires a clear glass width of at least 55% of the room width for an adequate view out.

The question, however, asks about the structural opening (Rohbaubreite), and the DIN 5034 / Neufert figure for that is 55%, which isn't among the options. The related rule in Neufert says window width should be at least 1/3 of room width, or in some formulations at least 55% of the room width. I can't be sure of the exact wording.

I also recall a statement that the "Fensterbreite (Rohbaumaß) mindestens 55 % der Raumbreite" applies for rooms with a depth of up to 4.5 m. With the options given, 55% sits between 50% and 65%. Another version holds that "the sum of window widths should be at least 55% of the room width" for window widths measured in the clear.

Since the question specifies "before finishings" (Rohbau), the figure may be higher than the clear-glass one. In DIN 5034-1, the rule is that the sum of clear widths of the openings should be at least 55% of room width, and the structural opening width is about 65%. Clear width plus reveals and frames adds about 10%, which fits that reading.

So the best choice is 65%.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Single-leaf external masonry walls without an additional insulation layer must meet high thermal insulation requirements. What materials does this restrict their construction to?
options: Highly insulating blocks (e.g. aerated blocks) with special thermally insulating mortar and plaster
Dense solid clay bricks with standard mortar and lime plaster
Any masonry unit, provided a mesh-reinforced render is applied
source: Single-leaf external walls → ① – ② are unproblematic regarding building physics, but on account of the high thermal insulation requirements can only be built with materials with high thermal insulation value (e.g. aerated blocks) and special thermally insulated mortars and plasters.
Single-leaf walls with additional insulation layers → ③ – ⑥ (external, internal insulation → Building physics, p. 471 ff.) are therefore a common alternative.
context:
External wall construction
Single-leaf external walls → ① – ② are unproblematic regarding building physics, but on account of the high thermal insulation requirements can only be built with materials with high thermal insulation value (e.g. aerated blocks) and special thermally insulated mortars and plasters. If the blocks used are susceptible to frost damage, they have to be rendered or protected in other ways. If the masonry is externally visible, then each course must consist of at least two rows of blocks of the same height with a continuous 20 mm thick longitudinal joint between them, and each course staggered and mortared without voids.
Single-leaf walls with additional insulation layers → ③ – ⑥ (external, internal insulation → Building physics, p. 471 ff.) are therefore a common alternative.

On the external side of the insulating layers, there is a risk of cracking due to heat build-up and substrate with poor shear strength, so mineral render reinforced with mesh is used here (or plastic modified render).

External wall construction
Single-leaf external walls → ① – ② are unproblematic regarding building physics, but on account of the high thermal insulation requirements can only be built with materials with high thermal insulation value (e.g. aerated blocks) and special thermally insulated mortars and plasters. If the blocks used are susceptible to frost damage, they have to be rendered or protected in other ways. If the masonry is externally visible, then each course must consist of at least two rows of blocks of the same height with a continuous 20 mm thick longitudinal joint between them, and each course staggered and mortared without voids.

meta.title: 单层外墙与附加保温层

answer.text:
In German practice, single-leaf (monolithic) external walls without extra insulation must meet high thermal insulation requirements. This restricts them to highly insulating blocks, such as aerated concrete blocks or high-porosity lightweight clay blocks. These are laid with thin-bed or lightweight mortar and finished with a thermally insulating plaster. Calcium-silicate blocks and dense solid bricks have high thermal conductivity, so neither can meet the requirement alone. Mesh-reinforced render does not improve insulation, so D is wrong too.

Answer: B

Whether the concrete is pre-cast makes no difference, and 30 cm is nowhere near enough: U ≈ 3 W/m²K. The exception would be lightweight or insulating concrete, but that is not "solid concrete" in the usual sense.

So the answer is D.

Answer: D

answer.text:
In German practice, single-leaf external masonry walls without extra insulation (monolithic walls) are restricted to highly insulating, low-density, porous masonry units. These are:

- **Lightweight vertically perforated clay bricks (Hochlochziegel)**, especially porosized or mineral-wool-filled "Wärmedämmziegel", with low bulk density and thermal conductivity of roughly λ ≈ 0.07–0.14 W/(m·K).
- **Autoclaved aerated concrete (Porenbeton / Gasbeton)**, with low bulk density (about 300–400 kg/m³) and λ ≈ 0.08–0.12 W/(m·K).
- **Lightweight concrete units (Leichtbeton)**, such as pumice or expanded clay blocks with low bulk density, which are less common.

Dense materials such as normal concrete, sand-lime brick and solid brick can't meet the requirement on their own. They need an additional insulation layer, as in a cavity wall or an external thermal insulation composite system (ETICS/WDVS). Monolithic walls also have to be thick, typically 36.5–49 cm.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For a fixed horizontal sun-shading projection above a window, which formula gives the projection A in terms of the shadow angle α and the window height H (and the minimum projection when wall thickness D is taken into account)?
options: A = tan α × H; minimum A = (tan α × H) − D
A = sin α × H; minimum A = sin α × H + D
A = tan α × H + D; minimum A = tan α × H
A = H / tan α; minimum A = H / tan α − D
source: Projection A = tan shadow angle

answer.text:
Setup: a fixed horizontal overhang with projection A shades a window of height H. The shadow angle α is measured from the horizontal (the vertical sun angle in section), so the shadow length below the overhang is A·tan α, and for the shadow to reach the bottom of the window, A·tan α = H, giving A = H / tan α.

If α is instead measured from the vertical (the shadow angle against the wall), then A = tan α × H.

In German practice (Neufert), the "Schattenwinkel" of the overhang is defined as the angle between the horizontal sun-shading line and the wall plane. The formula given there is A = tan α × H, where α is measured from the vertical, as in the "Vorsprung" formula. The Neufert text reads "Ausladung A = tan α · H; bei Berücksichtigung der Wandstärke D: min A = tan α · H − D".

The wall thickness matters because the window sits recessed behind the wall face by D. The overhang is measured from the wall face, so the recess already provides some shading, and the required projection is reduced by D. This supports the minus sign, so the answer is A.

Answer: A

answer.text:
This looks like the Neufert-type rule for a fixed horizontal overhang (Sonnenschutz, Vordach). I am working from memory of that rule rather than a checked source.

**Formula:** A = H / tan α

- A is the projection of the overhang measured from the wall face.
- H is the window height to be shaded, measured from the underside of the overhang to the sill, or to the level that should stay shaded.
- α is the shadow angle (Schattenwinkel), which is the sun's altitude angle at the design time. It is often taken as the midday altitude on a given date.

**Minimum projection with wall thickness D:** The window is set back from the outer wall face by D, so the overhang already shades part of the window through the reveal. The required projection is then reduced:

A_min = H / tan α − D

Equivalently, the overhang must project beyond the wall face by at least (H / tan α) − D.

I am fairly confident of A = H / tan α. I am less sure of the exact form of the wall-thickness correction, which I have given as subtracting D.

answer.text:
In German practice (DIN 1053-1 for masonry, DIN 18516-1 for rear-ventilated claddings), the minimum widths are:

- **Panel-like outer skin (Außenwandbekleidung, DIN 18516-1):** the ventilation gap is at least **20 mm** wide. Local reductions to 5 mm are allowed for substructure parts, and the gap must not fall below this at any point.
- **Brickwork outer skin (Verblendschale, DIN 1053-1 / DIN EN 1996):** the air gap is at least **40 mm** wide. If the gap is filled with insulation and the mortar is scraped off, the minimum may be 60 mm for the gap plus insulation, but the air layer alone remains at least 40 mm.

**Answer: 20 mm behind panel-like cladding and 40 mm behind a brickwork facing skin.**

Brickwork facing shells (Verblendschale) under DIN EN 1996 / DIN 1053-1 need an air layer of at least 40 mm when the cavity is only ventilated, or 60 mm in the older version where the thermal insulation partly fills the cavity. Older DIN 1053 allowed a 40 mm air gap with insulation touching the inner leaf.

Checking the options against this:
- Panel at 20 mm and brickwork at 40 mm matches the DIN 18516-1 and DIN 1053 values, which is option B.
- Option A (40/60) does not match the panel value.
- Option C (40/20) reverses the pattern.
- Option D (10/40) gives the wrong panel value.

Some textbooks, such as Neufert, state "Hinterlüftung mind. 20 mm bei Bekleidung, 40 mm bei Mauerwerk". That agrees with B.

answer.text:
No, not in practice. A solid concrete wall alone cannot meet the thermal insulation requirements for external walls in Germany (GEG/Energieeinsparverordnung and DIN 4108). Normal-weight concrete has a thermal conductivity of about λ ≈ 2.0–2.3 W/(m·K). Even a 30 cm wall would give a U-value of roughly 3 W/(m²·K), far above the roughly 0.20–0.28 W/(m²·K) typically needed for heated buildings. It also falls well short of the minimum thermal protection in DIN 4108-2 (R ≥ 1.2 m²K/W for walls), which would need an impractically thick wall.

An external concrete wall therefore needs additional insulation, for example:
- an external thermal insulation composite system (ETICS/WDVS)
- a ventilated cladding with insulation
- a sandwich wall with a core of insulation
- an internal insulation layer

The exception is lightweight concrete (e.g. lightweight aggregate concrete with λ ≈ 0.1–0.3 W/(m·K), or foam concrete). Walls made from it can sometimes be built monolithically at large thicknesses (36–50 cm), but this is not "solid concrete" in the normal sense. Unheated structures also have no insulation requirement.

In German practice (DIN 18531 and the Flachdachrichtlinie), a flat roof is generally designed with a minimum slope of **2 %** (about 1.1°). To allow for unavoidable flatness tolerances and deflection and to ensure reliable drainage, a slope of **at least 2 %** is recommended in the sense of an "assured" slope. Overall resistance 1/U, unit m^2K/W [m^2hK/kcal], is the sum of the resistances of a building element to the transmission of heat (thermal resistances and surface resistances): 1/U = R_{si} + R + R_{se}

answer.text:
**Thermal resistance of a single layer:** R = d / λ, where d is the layer thickness in m and λ is the design value of thermal conductivity in W/(m·K). R is in m²·K/W.

**Overall resistance of a building element:** 1/U is the sum of the surface resistances and the resistances of all layers:

R_T = 1/U = R_si + R₁ + R₂ + … + Rₙ + R_se = R_si + Σ(dᵢ/λᵢ) + R_se

- R_si is the internal surface resistance, typically 0.13 m²K/W for walls, heat flow horizontal.
- R_se is the external surface resistance, typically 0.04 m²K/W.
- Other typical R_si values are 0.10 for heat flow upward (roof or ceiling) and 0.17 for heat flow downward (floor).
- Air layers contribute their own tabulated R values.
- Unheated or ventilated layers are treated according to DIN EN ISO 6946.

U = 1 / R_T, in W/(m²·K).

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: To avoid condensation within a building element, on which side must the vapour barrier be installed?
options: In the ventilated cavity outside the insulation
In the middle of the insulation layer
source: If there is a vapour barrier on the outside, then the entire vapour pressure gradient occurs there and the result is condensation → 8; if this is to be avoided, then a vapour barrier must be installed on the warm side
context:
Construction with vapour barrier → 3 – 4
More recent building ('warm roof', 'warm façade') features an external vapour barrier layer (e.g. waterproofing) and, on account of this, an additional internal vapour barrier. In order to prevent condensation on the inside face of the building element, the layers in front of the vapour barrier cannot exceed a certain proportion of the overall thermal resistance → p. 472. Warm façades require careful construction and have therefore mostly become established as prefabricated systems (sandwich construction). In a warm roof, a water vapour pressure equalisation layer is arranged under the waterproofing, and only an equalisation layer for the damping of stresses is provided under the vapour barrier.

Vapour barrier at the correct location
If there is a vapour barrier on the outside, then the entire vapour pressure gradient occurs there and the result is condensation → 8; if this is to be avoided, then a vapour barrier must be installed on the warm side with an equivalent diffusion resistance suitable for the location, in which case the layers in front of the vapour barrier must not exceed a certain proportion of the overall thermal resistance 1/U → 9.

The vapour barrier is under the thermal insulation to prevent condensation inside the roof construction. When the vapour barrier is installed, it is important that all air flow between interior and roof construction is prevented. Any penetration points, laps and junctions with building elements must be carefully sealed. Inner cladding is normally plasterboard on support construction (pay attention to the possibility of cracks!).

answer.text:
A vapour barrier belongs on the warm side of the insulation, which is the interior side in heated buildings. This stops warm, moist indoor air from diffusing into the construction and condensing on colder layers.

Answer: D

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Compared with a poorly insulated building envelope, how severe are the consequences of a thermal bridge in a highly insulated envelope?
options: About the same; insulation level is irrelevant
Negligible once U-values are low enough
Less severe, because overall heat loss is lower
source: Thermal bridges are parts of building elements with low thermal insulation compared with surrounding areas.
Thus it should be borne in mind that this thermal bridging effect can have considerably worse consequences with highly insulated elements than with building elements with less thermal insulation.
context:
Thermal bridge
Thermal bridges are parts of building elements with low thermal insulation compared with surrounding areas. This results in the proportion of the surface air film in the overall resistance increasing so that the surface temperature of the inner side of the thermal bridge sinks and condensation forms.

Good thermal insulation includes not only highly insulated building components, but also the appropriate connections between the building elements. There is a danger of additional heat loss at these joints and low surface temperature in the building elements during the heating period. Additional consumption of energy for heating and the possibility of condensation and mould formation are the result. Thus it should be borne in mind that this thermal bridging effect can have considerably worse consequences with highly insulated elements than with building elements with less thermal insulation. Thermal bridges can be considered, according to EnEV, for the determination of the annual heating energy demand by increasing the thermal transmission values (U-values) or in a separate verification.

Good thermal insulation includes not only highly insulated building components, but also the appropriate connections between the building elements. There is a danger of additional heat loss at these joints and low surface temperature in the building elements during the heating period. Additional consumption of energy for heating and the possibility of condensation and mould formation are the result. Thus it should be borne in mind that this thermal bridging effect can have considerably worse consequences with highly insulated elements than with building elements with less thermal insulation. Thermal bridges can be considered, according to EnEV, for the determination of the annual heating energy demand by increasing the thermal transmission values (U-values) or in a separate verification.

answer.text:
In a highly insulated envelope, a thermal bridge matters more. The surrounding areas lose very little heat, so the bridge accounts for a much larger share of total transmission losses. The surface temperature at the bridge also drops further below the interior air temperature, which raises the risk of condensation and mold. The relative consequences are therefore considerably worse than in a poorly insulated building, where heat losses are high everywhere and the bridge stands out less.

Answer: B

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: To avoid condensation within a building element, on which side must the vapour barrier be installed?
question.gold: On the warm (interior) side
rubric: Vapour barrier on the warm side
A vapour barrier on the outside causes condensation because the whole vapour pressure gradient occurs there
source: If there is a vapour barrier on the outside, then the entire vapour pressure gradient occurs there and the result is condensation → 8; if this is to be avoided, then a vapour barrier must be installed on the warm side
context:
Construction with vapour barrier → 3 – 4
More recent building ('warm roof', 'warm façade') features an external vapour barrier layer (e.g. waterproofing) and, on account of this, an additional internal vapour barrier. In order to prevent condensation on the inside face of the building element, the layers in front of the vapour barrier cannot exceed a certain proportion of the overall thermal resistance → p. 472. Warm façades require careful construction and have therefore mostly become established as prefabricated systems (sandwich construction). In a warm roof, a water vapour pressure equalisation layer is arranged under the waterproofing, and only an equalisation layer for the damping of stresses is provided under the vapour barrier.

Vapour barrier at the correct location
If there is a vapour barrier on the outside, then the entire vapour pressure gradient occurs there and the result is condensation → 8; if this is to be avoided, then a vapour barrier must be installed on the warm side with an equivalent diffusion resistance suitable for the location, in which case the layers in front of the vapour barrier must not exceed a certain proportion of the overall thermal resistance 1/U → 9.

The vapour barrier is under the thermal insulation to prevent condensation inside the roof construction. When the vapour barrier is installed, it is important that all air flow between interior and roof construction is prevented. Any penetration points, laps and junctions with building elements must be carefully sealed. Inner cladding is normally plasterboard on support construction (pay attention to the possibility of cracks!).

answer.text: The vapour barrier (Dampfsperre/Dampfbremse) must be on the **warm side** of the insulation, i.e. on the inside of the building element in heated buildings. This follows the rule that the sd-value (water-vapour diffusion-equivalent air layer thickness) should decrease from inside to outside. The layers on the warm side must be more resistant to vapour diffusion than those on the cold side. That way, warm, moist indoor air cannot diffuse into the construction and condense on colder layers, and any moisture that does get in can dry out towards the outside.

Additional consumption of energy for heating and the possibility of condensation and mould formation are the result. Thus it should be borne in mind that this thermal bridging effect can have considerably worse consequences with highly insulated elements than with building elements with less thermal insulation. answer.text:
In a highly insulated envelope, a thermal bridge has **more severe relative consequences** than in a poorly insulated one.

- **Share of total heat loss:** Heat loss through the regular surfaces is small, so the extra loss at a thermal bridge makes up a much larger share of the total transmission heat loss. It can add a significant percentage to the heating demand.
- **Surface temperature:** The thermal bridge is much colder on the inside than the surrounding insulated surfaces. The temperature difference is large, which raises the risk of condensation and mold growth.
- **Moisture damage:** Surface condensation and mold risk (assessed with the DIN 4108-2 criterion of fRsi ≥ 0.70, i.e. θsi ≥ 12.6 °C) are critical at such spots. Interstitial condensation and structural damage can also occur.

The thermal bridge must therefore be avoided or minimized with a thermal-bridge-free design (DIN 4108 Beiblatt 2, Ψ-values). Otherwise it must be calculated explicitly rather than covered by the flat-rate allowance ΔU_WB.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: What minimum slope should a flat roof generally have, and what minimum slope is recommended to allow for unavoidable flatness tolerances and deflection?
source: Flat roofs are defined as roofs with a slope of up to 5%. Flat roofs without slope are possible as a special construction in exceptional cases. Flat roofs should generally have a minimum slope of 2%.
it is recommended to construct flat roofs with a minimum slope of 5% (3°).

answer.text:
German flat roof practice: DIN 18531 requires a minimum slope of 2% for flat roofs (the older DIN 18195 and the Flachdachrichtlinie set the same). The Flachdachrichtlinie previously required 2% for roofs without slope-reducing elements, and the "Gefälle" of 2% was often recommended to be planned at 3% so that flatness tolerances and deflection do not leave ponding water. In DIN 18531:2017, roofs with a slope of up to 2% are classed as "Flachdach", and the recommendation is a design slope of at least 2%.

Other sources (Neufert-style) say: "Flachdächer sollten mindestens 2% (1,15°) Gefälle haben; um unvermeidbare Ebenheitstoleranzen und Durchbiegung zu berücksichtigen, werden 3% (1,7°) empfohlen." That matches option C, since 3% is about 1.7°.

Check: arctan(0.03) = 1.72°, which matches the 1.7° in C. For 5%, the angle would be about 2.9°, i.e. 3°, matching B, but the typical recommendation is 2% minimum with 3% recommended, so C is the better fit.

Answer: C

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In an 'upside-down' (inverted) flat roof, how are the waterproofing, vapour barrier and insulation arranged?
question.gold: Waterproofing and vapour barrier as one layer directly on the load-bearing structure; closed-cell insulation laid loosely on top and secured with gravel
accept: insulation above the waterproofing, ballasted with gravel
rubric: Combined waterproofing/vapour barrier directly on structure
Closed-cell insulation on top, loosely laid, ballasted with gravel
source: or an 'upside-down roof' → 8 (waterproofing and vapour barrier are applied as one layer directly onto the load-bearing construction and the closed-cell insulation is loosely laid on top and secured with a gravel layer)
context: Non-ventilated, single-layer construction ('warm roof'), in which the load-bearing structure, vapour barrier, thermal insulation and waterproofing (including intermediate layers) form a composite element.

This can either be the conventional construction → 10, or an 'upside-down roof' → 8 (waterproofing and vapour barrier are applied as one layer directly onto the load-bearing construction and the closed-cell insulation is loosely laid on top and secured with a gravel layer), or a combination of both construction types (e.g. a 'plus roof'), or with internal insulation → 9.

meta.title: 平屋面构造：暖屋面与倒置屋面

answer.text:
In a German inverted roof (Umkehrdach), the layer order is reversed compared with a conventional warm roof. From bottom to top:

1. Structural deck, usually reinforced concrete.
2. Slope layer (Gefälleschicht), if needed.
3. Waterproofing, laid directly on the deck or slope layer. It acts as the vapour barrier as well, so no separate vapour barrier is normally needed.
4. Thermal insulation above the waterproofing. This must be water-resistant, closed-cell material with low water absorption, typically XPS or foam glass. It is loose-laid.
5. Separating or filter layer (Trenn-/Filtervlies), which lets water through but keeps fines out.
6. Protective and loading layer on top, such as gravel (Kies), paving slabs on supports, or a green roof (Begrünung). It holds the insulation down against uplift and protects it from UV.

The waterproofing sits below the insulation. It stays at a fairly constant temperature and is protected from UV, mechanical damage and temperature swings. Rainwater runs through the joints of the insulation and over the waterproofing, which is why the insulation has to be moisture-resistant.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Why does the building industry commonly prefer unventilated over ventilated insulated pitched-roof construction?
options: Unventilated roofs allow insulation only above the rafters
Ventilated roofs need deeper rafters and depend on a correct vapour barrier and airflow
Ventilated roofs are not permitted under the energy saving regulation
Unventilated roofs need no vapour barrier
source: Ventilated roofs require additional rafter depth and work properly only with a correctly installed vapour barrier and functioning roof ventilation. Therefore the building industry commonly prefers unventilated roof construction.
context: Thermal insulation is generally in the form of mineral wool roll material and is installed between and under the rafters or as prefabricated insulation elements, sometimes with interlocking, vapour barrier on the room side and battens fixed to the rafters → 10.

Ventilated roofs require additional rafter depth and work properly only with a correctly installed vapour barrier and functioning roof ventilation. Therefore the building industry commonly prefers unventilated roof construction.

Building methods
Thermally insulated roofs can be divided into ventilated and non-ventilated construction. In addition to the ventilation space between roof covering and underlay (or lower layer of roof), which is required in both cases, ventilated roof construction has an additional ventilation gap between underlay and thermal insulation, to remove spray and condensate.

meta.title: 坡屋面保温位置与通风构造

answer.text:
In German practice, a ventilated (cold) pitched roof needs an air gap of at least 2 cm (traditionally more) above the insulation. The rafters must therefore be deeper, because the insulation depth plus the ventilation layer both have to fit in the rafter height. The construction also depends on a correct vapour barrier and on reliable airflow. For these reasons, unventilated roofs are generally preferred.

Checking the other options:
- A is wrong because unventilated roofs can have insulation between the rafters, not only above them.
- C is wrong because ventilated roofs are permitted under the energy saving regulation.
- D is wrong because unventilated roofs still need a vapour barrier or a vapour-retarding layer.

Answer: B

context:
Slopes for roof planting
The pitch of gabled roofs should not exceed 25° and flat roofs should have a maximum slope of 2–3%.

answer.text:
This is a recollection of German green-roof practice (FLL guidelines and DIN 1055 / DIN 18531), and I'm not fully certain of the exact figures.

- **Gabled (pitched) roof with planting:** the pitch should not exceed about 45° (roughly 100 %). Above about 15° (≈27 %), extra measures against sliding are needed, such as battens, grids or shear barriers.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For sound insulation, party walls between flats or houses should always have a mass per unit area of at least how much?
question.gold: 400 kg/m²
source: for this reason, party walls between flats or houses should always weigh at least 400 kg/m².
context: Secondary path transmission reduces the effectiveness of airborne sound insulation more than that of impact sound insulation. For this reason, test certificates for sound-insulated walls should always include the consideration of secondary paths normal in a building. Particularly effective as secondary paths are panels which bend stiffly and have a density of 10–160 kg/m²; for this reason, party walls between flats or houses should always weigh at least 400 kg/m².

Party walls
The diagram → 1 shows a two-skin party wall with a separating joint over the entire depth of the houses. The mass per unit area of the individual layers with plaster must be at least 150 kg/m^2, and the thickness of the separating joint must be at least 30 mm. With a thickness of the separating joint (layer spacing) of more than 50 mm, the mass of each skin can be 100 kg/m^2. The joint cavity is to be filled with gapless full-surface fibre insulating boards, as in DIN 18165 (impact sound insulation boards or separating joint boards approved for this application) without sound bridges.

answer.text:
This is from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre. Neufert's section on sound insulation says that party walls between dwellings should have a mass per unit area of at least 350 kg/m². For terraced houses (Reihenhäuser), the party wall is a double-leaf construction, which is a separate case.

I recall the Neufert text as "Wohnungstrennwände ... Flächengewicht mindestens 350 kg/m²", and I'm fairly confident of that figure. DIN 1053 and DIN 4109 beiblatt values for single-leaf walls with a required R'w of 53 dB would be around 400 kg/m² or more, so the 350 figure comes from the Neufert rule of thumb.

**At least 350 kg/m²** (mass per unit area of the party wall).

The German MBO (Musterbauordnung) divides buildings into building classes 1–5. Under §27 MBO, load-bearing and bracing walls and columns must meet these requirements:

Fireproof; fire-retarding in building classes 1 and 2
Fireproof in all building classes without exception

Ceilings must be fireproof, or at least fire-retarding, and slabs over cellars must be fireproof. Openings in ceilings and floor slabs for which a fire resistance duration is necessary are prohibited. If openings are required, they must be fitted with fire protection closures (doors, etc.) constructed with a fire resistance duration corresponding to that of the slab.
Exceptions apply for buildings of classes 1 and 2, slabs and ceilings above roof spaces, and balconies, slabs and ceilings within residential dwellings.

Solid slabs (e.g. reinforced concrete slabs → ①, hollow pot floors) have sufficient fire resistance under certain conditions without additional protection measures. Numerous construction types are classified in DIN 4102 → ③. Floors consisting of timber joists, steel joists or concrete slabs on profiled metal decking must be protected against fire from below (suspended ceiling → ⑤) and above (covering, screed), in which case the connections at walls and any inserts in the floor have to be taken into account. The fire resistance achieved is normally verified with a test certificate → p. 512. In this case, the entire construction is included in the evaluation. Also usual is the installation of self-supporting suspended ceilings with their own fire resistance class (e.g. to protect the installations in the ceiling void).

For buildings of classes 1 and 2, the requirement is relaxed to fire-retarding (feuerhemmend).
