question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For separating walls between residential or commercial units, what fire resistance duration is required and how far up must the walls extend?
options: Always 30 minutes; up to the suspended ceiling
Fire resistance equal to the storey's load-bearing components; up to the structural slab (in roof spaces to the roof cladding)
Always 90 minutes; up to the underside of the roof insulation
Fire resistance equal to the storey's load-bearing components; up to the suspended ceiling
source: The fire resistance duration of separating walls between residential or commercial units (or units and rooms used otherwise) must correspond to the quality of the load-bearing components of the storey. These must extend to the structural slab (in roof spaces up to the roof cladding).
context:
Separating walls
The fire resistance duration of separating walls between residential or commercial units (or units and rooms used otherwise) must correspond to the quality of the load-bearing components of the storey. These must extend to the structural slab (in roof spaces up to the roof cladding). Openings are limited to the size and number required for their use and must be closed by components which are at least fire-retarding, sealed and self-closing.

meta.title: 住宅/商业单元之间的分隔墙

answer.text:
In the German model building code (MBO §29), separating walls (Trennwände) between usable units must have fire resistance equal to the load-bearing components of the storey. In roof spaces, a separating wall is only required if the units there are separated. The walls must extend from the structural floor slab to the structural slab above, and in roof spaces up to the roof cladding.

MBO §29(2): "Trennwände sind erforderlich zwischen Nutzungseinheiten sowie zwischen Nutzungseinheiten und anders genutzten Räumen... (3) Trennwände nach Absatz 2 Nr. 1 sind bis zur Rohdecke oder bis unter die Dachhaut zu führen." Option B reflects this. Suspended ceilings would not provide this, unless they are themselves fire-rated.

Answer: B

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For sound insulation, party walls between flats or houses should always have a mass per unit area of at least how much?
source: for this reason, party walls between flats or houses should always weigh at least 400 kg/m².
context: Secondary path transmission reduces the effectiveness of airborne sound insulation more than that of impact sound insulation. For this reason, test certificates for sound-insulated walls should always include the consideration of secondary paths normal in a building. Particularly effective as secondary paths are panels which bend stiffly and have a density of 10–160 kg/m²; for this reason, party walls between flats or houses should always weigh at least 400 kg/m².

Party walls
The diagram → 1 shows a two-skin party wall with a separating joint over the entire depth of the houses. The mass per unit area of the individual layers with plaster must be at least 150 kg/m^2, and the thickness of the separating joint must be at least 30 mm. With a thickness of the separating joint (layer spacing) of more than 50 mm, the mass of each skin can be 100 kg/m^2. The joint cavity is to be filled with gapless full-surface fibre insulating boards, as in DIN 18165 (impact sound insulation boards or separating joint boards approved for this application) without sound bridges.

answer.text:
In German practice, party walls between flats or houses are usually given as needing a mass per unit area of about 400 kg/m². I am recalling this from Neufert-style guidance and DIN 4109 values, not deriving it. I am not fully certain of it, because DIN 4109 Beiblatt 1 gives figures near 490 kg/m² for some single-leaf walls. The 150 kg/m² figure is the one usually quoted for each leaf of a double-leaf house party wall, so it does not fit a general minimum. Of the options, 400 kg/m² is the best match.

Answer: C

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Why does the building industry commonly prefer unventilated over ventilated insulated pitched-roof construction?
question.gold: Ventilated roofs need additional rafter depth and only work properly with a correctly installed vapour barrier and functioning roof ventilation
accept: Ventilated roofs need additional rafter depth and only work properly with a correctly installed vapour barrier and functioning roof ventilation
rubric: Depends on correctly installed vapour barrier and working ventilation
source: Ventilated roofs require additional rafter depth and work properly only with a correctly installed vapour barrier and functioning roof ventilation. Therefore the building industry commonly prefers unventilated roof construction.
context: Thermal insulation is generally in the form of mineral wool roll material and is installed between and under the rafters or as prefabricated insulation elements, sometimes with interlocking, vapour barrier on the room side and battens fixed to the rafters → 10.

Ventilated roofs require additional rafter depth and work properly only with a correctly installed vapour barrier and functioning roof ventilation. Therefore the building industry commonly prefers unventilated roof construction.

Building methods
Thermally insulated roofs can be divided into ventilated and non-ventilated construction. In addition to the ventilation space between roof covering and underlay (or lower layer of roof), which is required in both cases, ventilated roof construction has an additional ventilation gap between underlay and thermal insulation, to remove spray and condensate.

meta.title: 坡屋面保温位置与通风构造

answer.text:
In German practice, the unventilated pitched roof ("Warmdach", i.e. without a ventilation layer) is usually preferred because it is simpler and cheaper to build, and it allows the full rafter depth to be filled with insulation.

- **Rafter depth:** In a ventilated roof (DIN 4108-3 / the old "Kaltdach" design) a free ventilation gap of at least 2 cm (up to 4 cm or more, depending on roof pitch and rafter length) must be kept above the insulation. This reduces the usable insulation depth, so a higher-performance insulation or deeper rafters are needed to meet the thermal requirements (GEG).
- **Construction effort:** The ventilated design needs air inlets at the eaves and outlets at the ridge or hip. These openings complicate eaves, ridge, hips, valleys, roof windows, dormers and roof penetrations, and sometimes make them impossible to detail. Complex or low-pitched roofs are especially difficult.
- **Cost and robustness:** Unventilated roofs need fewer components and less detailing, which lowers the risk of defects. With a properly sealed, vapour-retarding layer (often a humidity-adaptive vapour barrier, "feuchtevariable Dampfbremse") on the warm side, the moisture risk is controlled.

In short, unventilated roofs allow full-depth insulation and simpler, cheaper detailing, provided the airtight and vapour-control layers are carefully executed.

question.text: Under the German model building code building classes, what fire-resistance quality must load-bearing and bracing walls and columns (above ground) have in building class 5, in class 4, and in classes 1–2?
question.gold: Class 5: fireproof (fire-resistant); class 4: highly fire-retarding; classes 1–2: fire-retarding
source: Load-bearing and bracing walls and columns must be constructed fireproof in buildings of class 5, highly fire-retarding in buildings of class 4 and fire-retarding in buildings of classes 1 and 2
context: Solid waste can be temporarily stored inside the building. Waste can be stored temporarily inside buildings with more than two flats or a usable area of 400 m² (building classes 3–5) only if the rubbish collection room complies with the following requirements:

Load-bearing and bracing walls and columns must be constructed fireproof in buildings of class 5, highly fire-retarding in buildings of class 4 and fire-retarding in buildings of classes 1 and 2). This does not apply to the uppermost storeys of roof spaces without occupied rooms above them and balconies. In cellars, they have to be constructed fireproof and, in buildings of classes 1 and 2, fire-retarding.

Load-bearing and bracing walls and columns must be constructed fireproof in buildings of class 5, highly fire-retarding in buildings of class 4 and fire-retarding in buildings of classes 1 and 2). This does not apply to the uppermost storeys of roof spaces without occupied rooms above them and balconies. In cellars, they have to be constructed fireproof and, in buildings of classes 1 and 2, fire-retarding.

meta.title: 建筑等级与承重墙耐火

answer.text:
Under the German Musterbauordnung (MBO § 27), the requirements for load-bearing and bracing walls and columns above ground are:

- **Building class 5** (above the high-rise threshold is a separate matter; this covers other buildings of normal height that are not small): **fire-resistant (feuerhemmend is not enough); fire-resistance F 90, i.e. fire-resistant and made of non-combustible materials** (feuerbeständig, in the main parts non-combustible). Under the MBO 2002 this is "feuerbeständig", and the load-bearing parts must be made of non-combustible materials (F 90-A).
- **Building class 4:** **highly fire-retardant (hochfeuerhemmend), F 60**. The MBO 2002 required F 60 with fire-retardant, non-combustible requirements in the main parts, and later versions allow timber construction at F 60-B or better.
- **Building classes 1–2:** **fire-retardant (feuerhemmend), F 30**, with no requirement for non-combustible materials.
- **Building class 3:** no requirement.

**Short answer:** class 5 is feuerbeständig (F 90), class 4 is hochfeuerhemmend (F 60), and classes 1–2 are feuerhemmend (F 30).

question.text: Under German building regulations, what fire-resistance quality must load-bearing and bracing walls and columns in cellars (basements) have, and what relaxation applies to building classes 1 and 2?
question.gold: Fireproof; in building classes 1 and 2 fire-retarding
source: In cellars, they have to be constructed fireproof and, in buildings of classes 1 and 2, fire-retarding.
Ceilings must be fireproof, or at least fire-retarding, and slabs over cellars must be fireproof.
context: Load-bearing and bracing walls and columns must be constructed fireproof in buildings of class 5, highly fire-retarding in buildings of class 4 and fire-retarding in buildings of classes 1 and 2). This does not apply to the uppermost storeys of roof spaces without occupied rooms above them and balconies. In cellars, they have to be constructed fireproof and, in buildings of classes 1 and 2, fire-retarding.

Ceilings must be fireproof, or at least fire-retarding, and slabs over cellars must be fireproof. Openings in ceilings and floor slabs for which a fire resistance duration is necessary are prohibited. If openings are required, they must be fitted with fire protection closures (doors, etc.) constructed with a fire resistance duration corresponding to that of the slab.
Exceptions apply for buildings of classes 1 and 2, slabs and ceilings above roof spaces, and balconies, slabs and ceilings within residential dwellings.

Solid slabs (e.g. reinforced concrete slabs → ①, hollow pot floors) have sufficient fire resistance under certain conditions without additional protection measures. Numerous construction types are classified in DIN 4102 → ③. Floors consisting of timber joists, steel joists or concrete slabs on profiled metal decking must be protected against fire from below (suspended ceiling → ⑤) and above (covering, screed), in which case the connections at walls and any inserts in the floor have to be taken into account. The fire resistance achieved is normally verified with a test certificate → p. 512. In this case, the entire construction is included in the evaluation. Also usual is the installation of self-supporting suspended ceilings with their own fire resistance class (e.g. to protect the installations in the ceiling void).

meta.title: 地下室墙体与楼板耐火

answer.text:
Under the Musterbauordnung (MBO § 27) and the corresponding Landesbauordnungen, load-bearing and bracing walls and columns in cellars (Kellergeschossen) must be **fire-resistant (feuerbeständig)**, that is, fire resistance class F 90 (REI 90) and made of non-combustible materials. In DIN 4102 terms this means F 90-AB, with the load-bearing parts non-combustible.

**Relaxation:** In buildings of building classes 1 and 2 (freestanding detached houses and similar small buildings, and buildings of up to two units with a height of up to 7 m), the load-bearing and bracing walls and columns in the cellar only need to be **fire-retardant (feuerhemmend)**, i.e. F 30 (R 30). This is the same standard as for the upper storeys.

answer.text:
In German building regulation (Musterbauordnung, MBO §29 and the state building codes), the rules for separating walls ("Trennwände") between usable units are:

- **Fire resistance:** The walls must be fire-resistant (feuerhemmend, F30) in general. In buildings of building class 4 and 5 (higher buildings), they must be fire-resistant for 90 minutes (REI 90 / F90), as with load-bearing and stiffening elements.
- **Extent:** They must extend from the top of the floor slab to the underside of the next solid ceiling, or to the roof skin. If they end at a roof, they must be continued through the roof space up to the roof covering. Openings must be limited to what is necessary and fitted with self-closing, fire-resistant closures (T30).

The usual requirement in practice, particularly in residential construction, is therefore **fire resistance of at least 30 minutes (F30/REI 30)**, rising to **90 minutes** in buildings of higher building classes. The walls must go **from floor to ceiling, or up to the roof covering**.

meta.title: 外墙及外墙饰面的燃烧性能

answer.text:
The Musterbauordnung (MBO) §28 states that external wall claddings, including insulation and substructure, must be made of at least "schwer entflammbar" (difficult to ignite, i.e., flame-retardant/low flammability) materials. The exception is buildings of building classes 1 and 2, where normally flammable materials are allowed.

The answer options are phrased as "Normally flammable" (normal entflammbar), "Easily flammable" (leicht entflammbar), and "Flame-resistant" (probably the translation of schwer entflammbar). So the best match is D.

Option A would be the answer for building classes 1 and 2, but the question excludes those buildings, so the requirement is the stricter one: schwer entflammbar.

Answer: D

answer.text:
Under the Musterbauordnung (MBO § 28) and the state building codes, the rule is:

Outer wall claddings, including their insulation and substructure/fastening, must be at least **low flammability (schwerentflammbar, class B1 under DIN 4102 / B-s3,d0 under DIN EN 13501-1)** for buildings other than building classes 1 and 2 (that is, for building classes 3 to 5, up to just below high-rise height).

For high-rise buildings, the requirement is stricter: non-combustible (nichtbrennbar, A1/A2-s1,d0) materials.

Buildings of classes 1 and 2 (detached houses and small buildings of up to two units and up to 400 m² per floor) only need normal flammability (normalentflammbar, B2 / E).

question.text: Under German building regulations, what are the minimum floor area, minimum ceiling height, and minimum window area (relative to room area) of a residential (habitable) room?
source: minimum requirements for floor area (8 m^2), ceiling height (2.40 m), orientation, ventilation and lighting (window area 1/8 of the room area)
context:
Requirements
Student flats are 'living places' and not considered as residential homes in the sense of the building regulations. The general requirements of the building regulations essentially concern residential rooms with minimum requirements for floor area (8 m^2), ceiling height (2.40 m), orientation, ventilation and lighting (window area 1/8 of the room area), accessibility requirements (i.e. for disabled people) and escape routes (two independent escape routes from each floor, one of which is a legally essential stairway). The state guidelines for student residences set recommended dimensions for living places (approx. 12 m^2 for single rooms and approx. 16 m^2 for flats). In addition to this, a certain area will be required for communal use.

answer.text:
German building regulations (the Landesbauordnungen, with the Musterbauordnung as a model) set the following for habitable rooms:

- **Ceiling height:** The MBO and most state codes require a clear height of 2.40 m for habitable rooms. Some states differ, for example NRW at 2.40 m and Bavaria at 2.40 m. Attic rooms are treated differently.
- **Window area:** The clear window opening area must be at least 1/8 of the room floor area. This is the standard Rohbaumaß rule.
- **Minimum floor area:** The Bauordnung itself does not set a minimum floor area for habitable rooms. Older rules, such as the Wohnungsbauförderung guidelines, gave about 8 m² for a living room and about 6 m² for a kitchen. Some textbooks cite 8 m² as the minimum for a habitable room, and a typical exam answer would be "8 m², 2.40 m, 1/8".

Option A matches that typical answer. Option C gives 6 m², which is closer to a kitchen or small room, so A is the better fit.

Answer: A

question.text: Under German building regulations, when a kitchen is a habitable room, what minimum clear ceiling height and what minimum window area (structural dimensions, relative to the net floor area) must it have?
source: As a habitable room, the kitchen must have a clear ceiling height of at least 2.40 m and a window area (structural dimensions) of at least 1/8 of the net floor area.
context: Kitchens and kitchenettes without windows are generally undesirable and only permissible if effective ventilation is guaranteed. As a habitable room, the kitchen must have a clear ceiling height of at least 2.40 m and a window area (structural dimensions) of at least 1/8 of the net floor area.

answer.text:
German model building code (MBO) §47: habitable rooms (Aufenthaltsräume) must have a clear height of at least 2.40 m. §48 (older versions) require window area of at least 1/8 of the net floor area (Rohbaumaße). The MBO 2002 states "Fensterfläche mindestens ein Achtel der Grundfläche des Raumes einschließlich der Räume Nebenräume, Rohbaumaße".

Under Neufert, the kitchen as a habitable room: ceiling height 2.40 m, window area 1/8 of floor area (structural dimensions). Option C.

Some states (e.g. NRW) use 2.40 m, with 1/8 window area. So C.

Answer: C

answer.text:
Under the Wohnflächenverordnung (WoFlV, § 4), the clear ceiling height decides how a floor area is counted:

- **2 m or more:** the area is counted in full (100 %).
- **At least 1 m but less than 2 m:** the area is counted at half (50 %).
- **Less than 1 m:** the area is not counted (0 %).

This applies especially to rooms with sloping ceilings, such as attic rooms.

Two related rules in the same section:
- Unheated conservatories (Wintergärten) and similar fully enclosed spaces are counted at 50 %.
- Balconies, loggias and terraces are usually counted at 25 %, and up to 50 % at most.

question.text: Under German building regulations, when a kitchen is a habitable room, what minimum clear ceiling height and what minimum window area (structural dimensions, relative to the net floor area) must it have?
question.gold: 2.40 m; 1/8 of the net floor area
rubric: Window area at least 1/8 of net floor area
source: As a habitable room, the kitchen must have a clear ceiling height of at least 2.40 m and a window area (structural dimensions) of at least 1/8 of the net floor area.
context: Kitchens and kitchenettes without windows are generally undesirable and only permissible if effective ventilation is guaranteed. As a habitable room, the kitchen must have a clear ceiling height of at least 2.40 m and a window area (structural dimensions) of at least 1/8 of the net floor area.

answer.text:
Under the German Model Building Code (MBO) and the state building codes (Landesbauordnungen), a kitchen that counts as a habitable room (Aufenthaltsraum) must meet the same requirements as other habitable rooms:

- **Minimum clear ceiling height:** 2.40 m (MBO § 47). Some states set different values, for example for attic rooms or existing buildings.
- **Minimum window area:** 1/8 of the net floor area (Grundfläche) of the room, measured as rough-opening (structural) dimensions (Rohbaumaße). This follows MBO § 47 and the corresponding state rules.

A kitchen without a window, or with only a small one, is therefore not a habitable room. It is treated as an interior kitchen and needs mechanical ventilation.

The German Wohnflächenverordnung (WoFlV) of 2004, §4, sets the rules for areas under sloping ceilings:

- Floor areas with a clear height of at least 2 m are counted in full.

- Areas under 1 m are not counted.

The same rules also give a separate treatment for unheated winter gardens and for balconies (typically a quarter, up to half). The 1 m and 2 m thresholds are the ones that apply to sloping ceilings.

The older II. Berechnungsverordnung used 2 m for full counting and 1–2 m for half counting, so it also matches. The 1.50 m and 2.30 m figures come from other systems, such as DIN 277 or Austrian and Swiss rules, so they do not apply here.

Option A matches the WoFlV.

question.text: Under German building regulations, what are the minimum floor area, minimum ceiling height, and minimum window area (relative to room area) of a residential (habitable) room?
question.gold: 8 m²; 2.40 m; window area 1/8 of room area
source: minimum requirements for floor area (8 m^2), ceiling height (2.40 m), orientation, ventilation and lighting (window area 1/8 of the room area)
context:
Requirements
Student flats are 'living places' and not considered as residential homes in the sense of the building regulations. The general requirements of the building regulations essentially concern residential rooms with minimum requirements for floor area (8 m^2), ceiling height (2.40 m), orientation, ventilation and lighting (window area 1/8 of the room area), accessibility requirements (i.e. for disabled people) and escape routes (two independent escape routes from each floor, one of which is a legally essential stairway). The state guidelines for student residences set recommended dimensions for living places (approx. 12 m^2 for single rooms and approx. 16 m^2 for flats). In addition to this, a certain area will be required for communal use.

answer.text:
Germany has no single national figure for these. The Musterbauordnung (MBO) and the state building codes (Landesbauordnungen, LBO) set them, and the values below are the commonly cited ones.

- **Ceiling height:** at least 2.40 m clear height in habitable rooms (MBO § 47). Rooms in attics and under sloping roofs may be lower in part, and some states set different values for existing buildings or special cases.
- **Floor area:** the MBO sets no explicit minimum area for a habitable room. Older DIN 283 and some state rules gave about 8 m² for a living room or bedroom (6 m² for a small single room), and about 6 m² for a kitchen. Under social housing standards (DIN 18011 and the Wohnflächenverordnung), the usual guide is about 10–12 m² for a living or bedroom space.
- **Window area:** the clear window opening (raw-opening/glazed area) must be at least 1/8 of the room's floor area (MBO § 47). Some state codes round this to 12.5%. Older practice used 1/10 of the floor area in some cases.

**Summary:** about 2.40 m ceiling height, about 8 m² minimum room area (a customary figure, not set in the MBO), and a window area of at least 1/8 (12.5%) of the floor area.

answer.text:
Under the Wohnflächenverordnung (WoFlV, 2003), a room's floor area is measured from the **finished surfaces of the room's enclosing walls**. This means the clear floor area is taken at the finished (plastered) wall surfaces, **not from the raw structural dimensions**. Plaster and wall cladding are therefore not counted as floor area, and the area is not taken from the unplastered shell dimensions as in the older II. BV method. The floor is measured at floor level, without the skirting boards.

Floor area beneath sloping ceilings is counted in full where the clear height is at least 2 m. It is counted at half where the height is between 1 m and 2 m, and it is not counted below 1 m. Balconies, terraces and similar areas are normally counted at 25%, and up to 50% at most.

The German Wohnflächenverordnung (WoFlV) of 2003, § 3, says floor area is determined from the dimensions of the "fertigen Oberflächen" (finished surfaces) of the room, i.e. the clear dimensions between finished wall surfaces. By contrast, DIN 277 uses the raw structural dimensions (Rohbaumaße), and the older II. Berechnungsverordnung allowed a plaster deduction from the raw dimensions.

Under WoFlV § 3 (Ermittlung der Grundfläche), the base area is determined either from the finished room dimensions between the plaster or cladding surfaces, or from the raw building dimensions with a 3% deduction for plaster. The rule is therefore the clear dimension to the finished surface, including plaster and cladding. Option D matches this: clear dimensions from the face of the building components' cladding.

Option B would describe the unfinished structural faces, but the WoFlV gives preference to the finished surfaces. Plaster is allowed to be accounted for through the 3% deduction only when the dimensions come from the building plans.

Option D is the best match.

Answer: D

In German design practice (Neufert, DIN 18040 and the usual dwelling-planning guidance), a balcony, loggia or terrace should be directly accessible from, and related to, the **living room**, which is the main living space. Under DIN 4109 (sound insulation in buildings), the noisy installations named here (water and waste pipes, lifts and so on) must not be placed in walls of rooms that need protection from noise. The Neufert-style rule is that installations are not placed in the walls of living rooms and bedrooms.

answer.text: Under the German state building codes (Landesbauordnungen, based on the Musterbauordnung), lifts are required in buildings with **more than five full floors**, meaning the floor level of the top storey is more than 13 m above ground level. The exact threshold differs slightly between states. Some require lifts from the fifth floor upward, and some, such as Berlin and Brandenburg, set stricter requirements. Where lifts are required, at least one must be able to carry wheelchairs, prams, and stretchers.

meta.title: DIN 277 建筑体积（总体积与净体积）

answer.text:
In DIN 277 (the 1987 version, and similar in the 2005 and 2016 versions), the gross volume (Brutto-Rauminhalt, BRI) is calculated from the gross floor area multiplied by the height. The height is measured from the top of the lowest structural floor (the upper surface of the floor construction or foundation slab) up to the upper surface of the roof or the top of the roof covering, or of the upper floor structure for the topmost level.

In the 1987 version, the BRI is the product of the plan area and the height between the underside of the lowest floor structure (the foundation slab) and the upper surface of the roof or top-level ceiling covering. The 2005 and 2016 versions are the same in principle: the volume is measured from the top of the lowest structural floor to the top of the roof covering or upper structure.

**Answer:** The height is measured from the upper surface of the lowest floor structure (the floor slab at the bottom of the building) up to the upper surface of the finished roof or top covering. In practice, the volume is taken between the underside or top of the lowest floor construction and the outer surface of the roof, as in the 1987 definition. The 2005/2016 wording is the one described here: from the top of the lowest floor structure to the top of the roof construction or covering.

question.text: Under German building regulations, residential buildings with more than how many full floors require lifts?
source: Lifts are required for residential buildings of more than five full floors
context: Lifts are required for residential buildings of more than five full floors → p. 128. If a residential building is more than 22 m above ground level, then the provisions for high-rise buildings apply → p. 244.

Two to four flats per floor → ② – ④
Two flats per floor is the most common access method, with balanced advantages of residential quality and value for money. The arrangement allows various (and flexible) floor plan solutions → ⑥ and offers good possibilities for adaptation in every compass direction.

answer.text:
In Germany, the model building code (MBO §39) requires lifts in buildings with more than 13 m of floor height (Fußboden of the top floor above ground). Many state building codes (Landesbauordnungen) specify lifts for buildings with more than 4 full floors (e.g., Bavaria: more than 5 full floors; NRW: more than 3 full floors; Berlin: more than 5 floors). The widely cited statement, as in Wikipedia's "Lift (elevator)" or "Barrierefreies Bauen", is that "In Germany, residential buildings with more than five full floors require lifts" — in the MBO, "Gebäude mit mehr als 5 Geschossen oberirdisch müssen Aufzüge haben" (MBO 2002 §39: "Gebäude mit mehr als fünf oberirdischen Geschossen müssen Aufzüge in ausreichender Zahl haben"). Older MBO versions said that for buildings with more than 4 full floors. The MBO 2002 wording is "mehr als fünf", though it was later changed to refer to Hochhausgrenze of 13 m. I'll go with five.

Answer: D

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In the grouped room floor plan for apartments (developed in the early 20th century), into which two room groups is the dwelling divided, and which rooms belong to each?

The idea of the grouped room floor plan developed at the start of the 20th century and is based on the separation of areas inside the apartment into two 'room groups': the living areas (living room, kitchen and dining area) and the sleeping area (bedrooms and bathrooms).

Central corridor plan → ①
The central corridor plan is the classic floor plan of late 19th-century urban apartment blocks. The rooms are arranged along the two façades and are separated by the (load-bearing) middle wall and the central corridor parallel to it. All rooms can be accessed and used separately. The "gruppierter Grundriss" in German housing design (Neufert and others) divides the dwelling into a Wohngruppe (living group) and a Schlafgruppe (sleeping group). The living group contains the living room, kitchen, and dining space. The sleeping group contains the bedrooms and the bathroom, with the WC and bath usually placed near the bedrooms.

Option D matches this division. Option C places the kitchen with the bedrooms, which is wrong. Option A uses a day/service split that does not match the grouped plan. Option B describes a corridor layout, not the grouped plan.

context:
Sound from services
Sound from services can occur as plumbing fixture sound, pipework sound or filling/emptying sounds. The maximum permissible sound level from services in neighbouring residential units is 35 dB (A). Noisy elements of services (water pipes, waste pipes, gas riser pipes, waste disposal units, lifts) may not be installed in the walls of rooms where quiet is required (living rooms, bedrooms).
Lifts should be installed in separate shafts (joints filled with >3 cm mineral fibre) → 7; otherwise, the top of the shaft should be elastically supported → 8.

answer.text:
In German practice (DIN 4109, as presented in Neufert), noisy installations and service elements such as water and waste pipes, gas risers, waste chutes and lifts should not be placed in or against the walls of rooms that need protection from noise. These are the **living rooms and bedrooms** (Wohn- und Schlafräume) of the dwelling itself, and also those of neighbouring dwellings. They should instead be located next to rooms that tolerate noise, such as kitchens, bathrooms, WCs and stairwells.

DIN 4109 also sets a maximum sound level of 30 dB(A) for noise from water installations in these rooms.

answer.text:
In German design practice (Neufert-based), the parents' bedroom is normally oriented to the **east** (or northeast/southeast), so it gets morning sun and stays cooler in the evening. Children's bedrooms, which double as play areas, are oriented to the **south or southeast/southwest**, so they get plenty of sun during the day.

Living rooms are normally oriented to the south or west, and kitchens to the north or east.

answer.text:
This is the "gruppierter Grundriss" in German apartment design (Neufert-style teaching). The dwelling is split into two zones:

1. **Tagesräume (day rooms / communal and living zone):** living room, dining room, kitchen (with the entrance area and the sitting or reception rooms). These are used by the whole household during the day.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In a house, which of the most important communal areas should be directly accessible from the entrance hall?

Entrance hall
The entrance hall should be enclosed where the entrance leads directly to the open air with an inner door (wind lobby function). It should also offer sufficient room for a lot of moving around → ④. This is where reception, greeting, taking off and putting on coats, and taking leave all take place, but also offers the first orientation for the visitor → ① – ③. In German design practice (Neufert-style guidance), the entrance hall (Diele/Flur) should give direct access to the main communal rooms: the **living room (Wohnzimmer)**, the **kitchen** (and usually the dining area), and normally the **WC/cloakroom** and stairs as well. The bedrooms and children's rooms are the private areas, reached via the stairs or a separate corridor.

My best answer: the living room, the kitchen (with dining room) and the guest WC should be directly accessible from the entrance hall.

This is where reception, greeting, taking off and putting on coats, and taking leave all take place, but also offers the first orientation for the visitor → ① – ③. Countless objects therefore have to be arranged practically yet tidily in this limited space → ⑤, ⑥. The most important communal areas like the kitchen, WC and staircase should be directly accessible from the entrance hall.

Entrance
The entrance is the face of a house, where visitors gain their first impression. A multitude of functions have to be practically arranged and appropriately designed → ①. If the entrance is into the open air, it should be protected from the prevailing wind direction if possible. If weather conditions are unfavourable, a lobby is also recommended to prevent wind blowing through → p. 136 (if the entrance is into a stair shaft, then this can provide wind protection).

answer.text:
This comes from Neufert-type guidance on dwelling entrances, and I'm answering from memory of that rule rather than a checked source.

An entrance hall (Diele or Flur) should be closed off from the rest of the dwelling by an inner door, such as a glazed door, so that it works as a wind lobby (Windfang). It should be closed off in this way when the front door opens directly to the outside, because draughts, cold air and noise would otherwise reach the living areas.

The inner door is unnecessary when the dwelling is entered from an enclosed, unheated but wind-protected area, such as an internal stairwell or access corridor in a multi-family building. A wind lobby is also unnecessary where the entrance is already sheltered, for example by a porch or an outer vestibule.

**Short answer:** Add an inner door (wind lobby) when the front door opens directly outdoors. Omit it when the dwelling is entered from an enclosed stairwell or corridor inside the building, as in apartment buildings.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: A detached, owner-occupied house on its own plot typically has direct access to private or semi-public open spaces (garden, terrace, courtyard, roof garden) from which storeys?

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Terraced (row) houses can receive direct daylight only from two façades. question.text: According to the German building regulations, apart from the bathroom, which two rooms belong to the mandatory provision of every house or flat?

Storerooms are used for keeping and storing cleaning equipment, tools, cleaning agents, shopping baskets, and bulky items like bags, suitcases, washing baskets and stepladders. answer.text:
This question appears to come from Neufert's Architects' Data, which discusses German state building codes (Landesbauordnungen). Under the Musterbauordnung, every dwelling must have a kitchen or kitchenette, a bathroom with a bath or shower, and a WC. Each dwelling must also have a storeroom (Abstellraum) of adequate size, and in multi-family buildings a bicycle and pram room.

The question asks for two rooms besides the bathroom. Option D, "a kitchen or kitchenette, and a sufficiently large storeroom," matches that provision. Option A (a guest WC) is not required, option B (a laundry room) is not required, and option C (a separate dining room) is not required either.

Answer: D

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: What building-services provision do open kitchens (kitchens open to the living/dining space of a dwelling) require, and for what reason?
question.gold: Good ventilation and extraction, so cooking smells do not impair the living and dining areas
accept: good ventilation and an extractor, so cooking smells stay out of the living/dining area
effective air extraction/ventilation against cooking smells
rubric: Purpose: avoid cooking smells in living/dining areas
source: Open kitchens require good ventilation and extraction in order not to impair the living and dining room areas with cooking smells.
context: Modern kitchen designs are moving away from the fitted kitchen. The kitchen area is seen as an ensemble of independent objects developed in each case from formal and functional conditions, which are grouped like pieces of furniture in an (ideally generous) residential room. Open kitchens require good ventilation and extraction in order not to impair the living and dining room areas with cooking smells. In many cases, a mobile divider is to be recommended, for example using a curtain → 9.

answer.text:
In German design practice (as in Neufert), an open kitchen needs an extractor hood, ideally a powerful one that vents to the outside (or a recirculating unit with filters), plus adequate ventilation. The reason is that cooking odours, grease-laden vapour, moisture and heat would otherwise spread into the living and dining area. This would affect comfort and hygiene, deposit grease on furnishings and surfaces, and raise the humidity, which risks mould. For the same reason, the ventilation concept (DIN 1946-6) must be checked, especially with airtight buildings. An exhaust-air hood in an open kitchen also needs a supply of replacement air, and this has to be coordinated with any fireplace in the home.

**Short answer:** Open kitchens need an effective extractor hood or mechanical ventilation, to remove cooking odours, grease and moisture so they do not spread into the living area.

This appears to come from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre, which lists the bathroom types as follows:

- (Guest) WC: WC and washbasin.
- Shower room (Duschbad): shower, washbasin and WC.
- Bathroom (Badezimmer): bath, washbasin and WC.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For technical reasons, the bathroom (or WC) of a dwelling is often conveniently placed on a common installation shaft together with which other room?

In larger houses, bath and WC should be in separate rooms, or an additional WC (guest WC) should be provided. The bathroom should be oriented to the north, and if possible have natural ventilation and lighting (otherwise provide effective mechanical ventilation according to DIN 18017-3). The bathroom is normally next to the bedroom → ⑤ – ⑥, ⑧ – ⑩, although it is also often convenient for technical reasons to place bath and kitchen (or WC and kitchen) on a common installation shaft → ⑧ – ⑨.

answer.text:
Wet rooms (the bathroom or WC and the kitchen) are usually grouped around a common installation shaft so that the supply and drain pipes can be shared. This is the standard recommendation in German planning guides such as Neufert.

Answer: A

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In residential planning, in which room are wardrobes and linen cupboards normally situated in a dwelling, and what provision does a walk-in wardrobe additionally require?
question.gold: In the bedroom; walk-in wardrobes require appropriate ventilation
source: They serve to store (larger) items of clothing, linen, shoes and suitcases, and are normally situated in the bedroom.
Walk-in wardrobes also require appropriate ventilation
context:
Details and fitting out
Wardrobes and linen cupboards are an essential part of fitting out a home. They serve to store (larger) items of clothing, linen, shoes and suitcases, and are normally situated in the bedroom.

When wardrobes are sited along external walls, care should be taken that the thermal insulation is adequate and that ventilation is provided. Walk-in wardrobes also require appropriate ventilation → 4.

answer.text:
In German residential planning (Neufert/DIN-based practice), wardrobes and linen cupboards are normally placed in the bedroom (Schlafzimmer), often as built-in or fitted units along a wall, or in an adjoining dressing area.

A walk-in wardrobe (begehbarer Kleiderschrank / Ankleideraum) additionally needs its own sufficient circulation and standing space inside, i.e. a clear access and movement area in front of the cupboards, and in practice also ventilation (a window or mechanical ventilation) because it is a closed room without natural airing. I'm not fully certain of the exact point the source intends, but the answer is: bedroom, and for a walk-in wardrobe, ventilation (an air exchange provision) plus enough free floor space to move and dress.

answer.text:
Neufert-style rule: a bathroom should ideally face north (or northeast), since it needs little sunlight and stays cooler. Where natural lighting and ventilation through a window aren't possible (an internal bathroom), effective mechanical ventilation must be provided according to DIN 18017 (Lüftung von Bädern und Toilettenräumen ohne Außenfenster – DIN 18017-3 covers fan-based ventilation, and DIN 18017-1 covers shaft ventilation).

**Answer:** North (north/northeast side); mechanical ventilation per DIN 18017 (ventilation of bathrooms and WCs without external windows).

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Residential bathrooms are commonly divided into four basic categories: (guest) WC, shower room, bathroom and full bathroom. Which fittings does a 'full bathroom' contain?
question.gold: Bath, shower, washbasin and WC
source: The basic bathroom categories are: (guest) WCs with WC and washbasin → 3 - 4, shower rooms with shower and basin → 5 - 6, bathrooms with bath, washbasin and WC → 7 - 8, full bathrooms with bath, shower, washbasin and WC → 10.
context: The basic bathroom categories are: (guest) WCs with WC and washbasin → 3 - 4, shower rooms with shower and basin → 5 - 6, bathrooms with bath, washbasin and WC → 7 - 8, full bathrooms with bath, shower, washbasin and WC → 10.

answer.text:
In German practice (as in Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre), a "full bathroom" (Vollbad / Vollbadezimmer) contains the following fittings:

- Bathtub
- Shower (separate from the tub)
- Washbasin, often a double basin
- WC
- Often a bidet as well

By comparison:
- A guest WC has a WC and a small washbasin.
- A shower room has a shower, a washbasin and a WC.
- A bathroom has a bathtub, a washbasin and a WC.

The full bathroom adds a separate shower to the bathroom's fittings. In the Neufert-style classification it is usually described as having a bathtub, a shower, a washbasin and a WC, with a bidet or a second basin as optional extras. It also commonly has connections for a washing machine.

answer.text:
This question most likely comes from the Neufert Bauentwurfslehre, and the underlying rule is in the Musterbauordnung (MBO) and the Landesbauordnungen.

MBO §49 (2) requires, for buildings with more than two dwellings, an easily accessible storage room for prams and bicycles (the wording in MBO 2002 is "Abstellräume für Kinderwagen und Fahrräder"). The "more than two dwellings" threshold lines up with building classes 3–5, since building class 1 is detached buildings and class 2 is buildings with up to two dwellings.

The number of vehicles is the harder part. Neufert says something like "For residential buildings of building classes 3-5, easily accessible communal storerooms for prams, pushchairs and bicycles are required; assume at least one bicycle per room/dwelling...". I don't recall an exact figure. Many state regulations (e.g. Berlin) require bicycle spaces per dwelling, and older rules asked for one space per dwelling. The per-dwelling basis is also the more standard design guidance.

Between A and B, I'll go with B: classes 3–5, one vehicle per dwelling.

Answer: B

The question seems to refer to the German Arbeitsstättenverordnung (ArbStättV) and its technical rules (ASR A1.2). Neufert-style tables list room heights for workplaces by floor area: up to 50 m² the height is 2.50 m, up to 100 m² it is 2.75 m, up to 250 m² it is 3.00 m, and so on.

The older Arbeitsstättenverordnung used a different table, and a "Vst" abbreviation might come from "Versammlungsstättenverordnung" or "Verkaufsstättenverordnung," but the question says workplace regulation.

The options show 2.75 m, 2.50 m, and either 2.10 m or 2.30 m. The old ArbStättV said that a reduced height of 2.50 m was allowed for predominantly sedentary activities, and that corridors and sanitary rooms could be 2.50 m. In the old ArbStättV §19 and the Neufert text, the 2.75 m height applied to rooms with 100 m² or less, and the minimum was 2.50 m in offices. The clear height for corridors and sanitary rooms was 2.50 m in the old rules. Option D gives 3.00, 2.75, 2.50, which does not match.

Of the remaining options, 2.75 m with a minimum of 2.50 m is the pattern that fits the old standard for office rooms. For corridors, the old rule said they may be lower, and for sanitary rooms (the building code) a height of 2.30 m is plausible, since the Musterbauordnung and many state building codes require 2.40 m for habitable rooms and 2.20 m for basements. Of the two, 2.30 m seems more likely than 2.10 m for sanitary and corridor rooms. I'm going with B.

Answer: B

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Approximately how many workstations does a group office have, and how many workstations characterise the large-scale open-plan office landscapes made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation?
source: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations
The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department.
Large-scale office landscapes with 100 or more workstations are made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation
context:
Group office: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department. This arrangement is preferred above all for creative, design or coordination and development activities with high internal communication needs.
→ 2

Group office: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department. This arrangement is preferred above all for creative, design or coordination and development activities with high internal communication needs.
→ 2

Open-plan office: A form of office developed in the 1960s and 1970s of the last century. Large-scale office landscapes with 100 or more workstations are made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation; they stand for free communication and openness. Economical cubic structures, however, have the disadvantage of high maintenance costs. This form is not very popular among users → 3.

Single-room offices are suitable for independent or concentrated work, as a single-person room or for a few people in very small groups who need to exchange information constantly. This arrangement has been common in Germany since World War II and still has its justification when the requirements of the workplace correspond (→ Gruner, Jahr; Steidle, Kissler; or → new offices for the Federal Environment Office, Dessau, Sauerbruch, Hutton) or in newbuild high-rise offices, where the structure of the building can be so decisive that it leads to the very standardised character of spatial and organisational working practices.

A more sensitive relationship to the direct working environment is closely linked to the predominant value orientation in the company. This is reflected in the attitude to the quality of the workplace (daylight, environmental context, energy consumption), and the activity (ecological viewpoints, material use, waste disposal). The workplace is an important place for social interaction among the users, which is increasing in relevance due to formalised work structures (IT, work organisation etc.). Increased mental and physical stress leads to a greater awareness of the working environment (sufficient space, some personal choice in furnishings, ventilation, lighting, sufficient protection from disruptions). 75% of daily work takes place at the 'close and extended workplace' → ②. Necessary work contacts and collectively used facilities are significant, thus the requirement for a mixed provision of single and group rooms, 'personal' and 'collective' workplaces → ③ – ④. In addition to the refurbishment of existing office space, new spatial concepts involving single and group rooms are starting to appear (Fuchs, Gottschalk, Henkel → refs).

answer.text:
This appears to come from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre, which describes office types. The text there reads roughly: "Zellenbüro (1–3 Arbeitsplätze), Gruppenbüro (4–16 Arbeitsplätze), Großraumbüro (ab 25 Arbeitsplätze)..." Another version of the text says: "Gruppenbüros mit ca. 4–16 Arbeitsplätzen... Großraumbüros mit 100 und mehr Arbeitsplätzen, die durch künstliche Beleuchtung und Belüftung möglich wurden."

I recall that in Neufert's discussion of the office landscape ("Bürolandschaft"), large rooms hold 100 or more workstations. The group-office range of 4–16 matches both A and D, so the open-plan figure decides between them. Neufert's text on the large open-plan office says "Großraumbüros mit mehr als 100 Arbeitsplätzen," which supports A.

Answer: A

answer.text:
This is from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre, which describes office types by size:

- **Group office** (Gruppenraum): approximately 4–6 workstations in some sources, but in Neufert the group office is given as about **10–25 workstations**.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In office planning, which grid module dimensions have proved successful in recent years for (a) single-room offices and (b) office types based on the combi principle?
question.gold: 1.50 m for single-room offices; 1.35 m for combi-offices
source: The modular dimensions, which have proved successful in recent years, are 1.50 m for single-room offices and 1.35 m for office types based on the combi principle.
context: Grid module spacings define possible room sizes through the resulting spacing of columns and façades. The fitting out and façade grids must be the same in order to enable the partitions to connect to the windows. The structural grid can be offset against the fitting out grid. This reduces the problem of connecting the partitions to columns, but loses space in the rooms, which contain columns. Because of the different lifecycles of the building elements, an adaptable module dimension should be chosen. The modular dimensions, which have proved successful in recent years, are 1.50 m for single-room offices and 1.35 m for office types based on the combi principle.

Modular dimension 1.50 m
This is the economical module dimension for single-room offices consisting mainly of double workstations. Workstation depth 2.20 m (80 cm desk, 1 m movement area, 40 cm shelf behind). With 10 cm wall thickness, this gives 4.40 m clear room space.

Modular dimension 1.35 m
Room widths of 3.80 m (~18 m^2 usable area) enable:
– additional filing storage; two computer workstations with a depth of 0.90 m, as recommended by accident insurance companies; one drawing board or drawing machine and one desk; one desk and meeting table for four people. answer.text:
This is from Neufert (Bauentwurfslehre), where the office section discusses axial grid dimensions. As I recall it, the proven grid module for single-room (cellular) offices is 1.20 m axis spacing, giving room widths of 3.60 m, 4.80 m, etc. Neufert also mentions 1.25 m as a common module, and I am less sure of that figure.

For combi offices, the figure is likely a larger grid of 1.50 m, or perhaps 1.80 m.

My best recollection of the Neufert wording is: "In den letzten Jahren haben sich bei Einzelbüros Rastermaße von 1,20 m bis 1,35 m bewährt, bei Kombibüros 1,50 m bis 1,60 m." (In recent years, grid dimensions of 1.20 m to 1.35 m have proved successful for single-room offices, and 1.50 m to 1.60 m for combi offices.) I am fairly unsure of these exact numbers.

I'll go with this recollection.

**Answer:**
- (a) Single-room offices: grid module of about 1.20 m to 1.35 m (commonly 1.25 m).
- (b) Combi offices: larger grid module of about 1.50 m to 1.60 m (some sources give 1.80 m).

question.text: According to the German building regulations, for residential buildings of which building classes is an easily accessible communal storeroom for prams, pushchairs and bicycles required, and how many vehicles should be assumed when designing it?
question.gold: Building classes 3–5; at least one vehicle per occupant (including children)
accept: classes 3 to 5; ≥1 vehicle per resident incl. children
rubric: Design for at least one vehicle per occupant, children included
source: for residential buildings in building classes 3–5, the building regulations require an easily accessible (communal) storeroom for prams, pushchairs and bicycles.
it can be assumed that at least one vehicle per occupant (including children) has to be accommodated
context:
Communal storerooms
In addition to the storerooms or storage spaces in each flat, for residential buildings in building classes 3–5, the building regulations require an easily accessible (communal) storeroom for prams, pushchairs and bicycles. Corresponding areas should also be provided in other residential buildings and detached houses.

Solid waste can be temporarily stored inside the building. Waste can be stored temporarily inside buildings with more than two flats or a usable area of 400 m² (building classes 3–5) only if the rubbish collection room complies with the following requirements:

For the design of these rooms, it can be assumed that at least one vehicle per occupant (including children) has to be accommodated. In addition to bicycles, prams and pushchairs, it is also necessary to consider mopeds, tricycles, trailers etc. → ①.

The rooms should if possible be located at street level, be lockable and equipped with hooks and bicycle stands to secure the stored vehicles. They can be laid out as storerooms inside the building (with access to the entrance) or as separate bicycle sheds → ② – ③. A sufficient number of additional bicycle stands should be provided in the open air, particularly if the storeroom has been situated in the cellar.

answer.text: Easily accessible communal storerooms for prams/pushchairs and bicycles are required in residential buildings of building classes 3 to 5, that is, buildings with more than two dwellings. answer.text:
This question appears to come from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre, which says that cleaner's rooms (Putzmittelräume/Reinigungsräume) should be provided on every floor, ideally with a water connection and a bucket sink (Ausgussbecken).

Option C matches this. The other options give the wrong frequency (one per 1000 m², one per building, or one every second floor) or the wrong fittings (no water supply, a washing machine).

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For good room acoustics, what are the guideline room volumes per person for rooms used for speech and for (concert) music?

answer.text:
According to Neufert (DIN-based practice), the guideline room volume per person is:

- **Speech** (lecture halls, classrooms, theatres for spoken word): about **3–6 m³ per person**, with roughly 4–6 m³ often given as the optimum.
- **Music** (concert halls): about **8–12 m³ per person**, with roughly 10 m³ as a typical value.

In short: roughly 4–6 m³/person for speech and 8–12 m³/person for concert music. I am less sure of the exact edges of these ranges than of the overall pattern that music needs about twice the volume speech does.

answer.text:
I recall the German Arbeitsstättenverordnung (ArbStättV) and its technical rule ASR A4.1 on sanitary rooms.

Toilets must be reachable from every workstation within 50 m, and the route must not cross open air. They must also be on the same floor.

For separate facilities, the rule is that separate toilet rooms for women and men are to be provided, or separate use must be possible. The Neufassung says that if more than 10 employees are present, separate toilet rooms must be provided (ASR A4.1: "Toilettenräume sind für Frauen und Männer getrennt einzurichten" with the exception of up to 9 employees, where one room is allowed if it can be locked). So the threshold is more than 10.

For washbasins, a handwashing basin must be provided in or near each toilet room. The architectural rule-of-thumb (Neufert) is one washbasin per 3 WCs. Option C matches on the 50 m figure, the more-than-10 threshold, and a ratio of that kind.

Answer: C

**Frequency:** provide one cleaner's room (Reinigungsraum/Putzmittelraum) on each floor. Where floors are large, provide one per cleaning section, roughly one per 1,000–1,500 m² of floor area.

answer.text:
This is from Neufert (Bauentwurfslehre), which covers registries and filing rooms. The usual figures:

- **Ceiling clearance height:** about 2.00–2.50 m for filing areas, so that two storeys of normal office space (about 3.00 m each) equal three storeys of filing. I believe the figure Neufert gives is a clear height of roughly 2.25 m, which fits that 2:3 ratio.
- **Floor loading:** archive rooms with mobile shelving should be designed for about 12.5 kN/m². DIN 1055 gives 5 kN/m² for ordinary archives and filing rooms, and mobile shelving is commonly designed for 7.5 kN/m² or more, which is why I'm unsure of the 12.5 figure.

**Answer:** a clear height of about 2.25 m, which gives 3 filing storeys for every 2 office storeys, and a floor load of about 12.5 kN/m² for mobile shelving.

answer.text:
In German design practice (e.g., Neufert), the entrance area of an office building is the link between the public outside and the internal working areas. It typically contains:

- **Entrance and lobby (Foyer/Eingangshalle):** a weather-protected entrance, usually with a wind lock (Windfang) or revolving/automatic doors, and an arrival and waiting zone.
- **Reception/porter's lodge (Empfang/Pforte):** visitor registration, information, switchboard and telephone, and security and access control (badges, turnstiles, barriers).
- **Waiting and visitor areas:** seating and a visitor-management zone.
- **Circulation and distribution:** the central distribution point to stairs, lifts, corridors and the individual departments, with barrier-free access (ramps, lifts).
- **Supporting functions:** cloakroom/coat storage, WCs (including accessible WCs), mail and parcel reception, and often a small café or catering area, an information display or exhibition space, and a link to meeting or conference rooms.
- **Technical and safety functions:** fire-safety and escape routes, signage, and sometimes building control and security rooms.

In short, the entrance area handles reception and information, access control and security, waiting, and distribution of people to the workspaces.

The question seems to come from German workplace regulations (ArbStättV / ASR A4.2 Pausen- und Bereitschaftsräume). question.text: Under German building regulations for office access systems: below what floor area of a combined use unit are the corridors inside it not subject to the requirements for escape routes?
source: For combined use units of less than 400 m², the corridors are not subject to the requirements for escape routes.
context:
Access systems
Fixed points are sanitary facilities, stairwells, lift shafts etc., situated at maximum spacings defined in the building regulations → 8 – 12. The arrangement of these determines urban development’s building structure → 7 – 16. For combined use units of less than 400 m², the corridors are not subject to the requirements for escape routes.

meta.title: 小型使用单元内的走廊

answer.text:
This matches the German Muster-Bauordnung (MBO) and the Muster-Verwaltungsvorschrift, as well as the Bavarian BayBO. Under MBO § 36, corridors "innerhalb von Nutzungseinheiten zur Nutzung durch einen Betrieb oder eine Organisationseinheit mit nicht mehr als 200 m²" do not need to be notwendige Flure. For offices in the Muster-Hochhausrichtlinie, "Nutzungseinheiten mit nicht mehr als 200 m²" are mentioned. Under MBO § 36 (1) there are exemptions from the notwendige Flure requirements: "Flure innerhalb von Wohnungen oder Nutzungseinheiten mit nicht mehr als 200 m² ..." That is the rule I'm recalling.

The question's wording, "combined use unit" (Nutzungseinheit), refers to an office use unit. In MBO § 36 (1), notwendige Flure are not required in Wohngebäuden geringer Höhe, and within Nutzungseinheiten with no more than 200 m². The Muster-Bauordnung also says "Nutzungseinheiten mit nicht mehr als 200 m², Flure innerhalb dieser Nutzungseinheiten," which fits. The 400 m² figure appears in the Muster-Verwaltungsvorschrift for Büro- und Verwaltungsgebäude with office units up to 400 m², but the MBO says 200 m². In MBO 2002, § 36(1) reads: "Flure innerhalb von Nutzungseinheiten zur Nutzung durch einen Betrieb oder eine Organisationseinheit mit nicht mehr als 200 m²" (in the Sonderbau context, 400 m² for Schulen). The 200 m² figure is the one in § 36.

Answer: D

answer.text:
In the German Muster-Bauordnung (MBO § 36) and the Arbeitsstättenverordnung/ASR A2.3, the rule that matters here is the exception for corridors in "Nutzungseinheiten". The MBO states that the requirements for "notwendige Flure" do not apply to corridors within a Nutzungseinheit with an area of at most 200 m² (§ 36 Abs. 1 Nr. 1). For Nutzungseinheiten of offices or administrative use, the MBO specifies that corridors within a Nutzungseinheit up to 400 m² are not required to be "notwendige Flure". This follows the wording of MBO § 36 (1): "Notwendige Flure sind nicht erforderlich: 1. in Wohngebäuden der Gebäudeklassen 1 und 2, 2. innerhalb von Wohnungen oder innerhalb von Nutzungseinheiten vergleichbarer Größe, 3. innerhalb von Nutzungseinheiten, die einen Brutto-Grundfläche von nicht mehr als 200 m² haben, 4. innerhalb von Nutzungseinheiten, die einer Büro- oder Verwaltungsnutzung dienen, mit nicht mehr als 400 m² Grundfläche; das gilt auch für Teile größerer Nutzungseinheiten, wenn diese Teile nicht größer als 400 m² sind, Trennwände die Anforderungen an notwendige Flure erfüllen..."

The question's "office access systems" wording points toward office/administrative use with the 400 m² threshold.

**Answer: 400 m²** – corridors within an office/administrative use unit smaller than about 400 m² (MBO § 36) are not required to meet the "notwendige Flure" (escape route corridor) requirements. For ordinary use units, the threshold is 200 m².

question.text: According to the German high-rise building regulations: (a) above what height of the uppermost floor (on one side of the building, above ground level) does a building intended for long-term human occupation count as a high-rise building, and (b) what minimum walking width must each of the emergency stairs have in a high-rise building up to 60 m high?
source: High-rise buildings are those intended for long-term human occupation whose upper-most floor on one side of the building is more than 22 m above ground level.
High-rise buildings up to 60 m high: at least two emergency stairs must be available, which must be located opposite in two separate fire compartments. Their walking width must be at least 1.25 m.
context:
Definition of high-rise buildings
High-rise buildings are those intended for long-term human occupation whose upper-most floor on one side of the building is more than 22 m above ground level.

Stairs
High-rise buildings up to 60 m high: at least two emergency stairs must be available, which must be located opposite in two separate fire compartments. Their walking width must be at least 1.25 m. The wellhole must be min. 0.80 m wide in order to avoid having to lay hoses on the stairs. Smoke outlets must be provided at their highest point (5% of the floor area but min. 1 m^2). The exit must be directly into the open air or through a lobby without any fire load. In exceptional cases, one staircase can be approved for high-rise buildings up to 60 m in height, if it is a safety staircase. Requirements for the location of stairs → 2 – 5.

answer.text:
A high-rise is a building whose uppermost floor is more than 22 m above ground level. For buildings up to 60 m high, each emergency stair must have a minimum walking width of 1.25 m.

Answer: B

I'm not fully certain of the star threshold, so treat the 3-star answer as my best estimate.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For a comfortable stair with the lowest energy requirement, a standard design rule combines riser height r and tread depth t, based on the stride length of an adult. Within what range should 2r + t lie?
source: In order to determine a suitable pitch with the lowest energy requirement, this formula applies: 2 r + t = 59–65 cm.
context: The experience of using stairs and access routes is very varied: from the creative possibilities of the most diverse residential stairs to an elaborate outside staircase, which one can stride up and down. Climbing stairs takes on average seven times the energy input as walking on the flat. The pitch is determined by the stride length of an adult (approx. 59–65 cm). In order to determine a suitable pitch with the lowest energy requirement, this formula applies: 2 r + t = 59–65 cm.

The standard step rule is \(2r + t \approx 63\) cm, typically within 59–65 cm.

question.text: According to the German high-rise building regulations: (a) above what height of the uppermost floor (on one side of the building, above ground level) does a building intended for long-term human occupation count as a high-rise building, and (b) what minimum walking width must each of the emergency stairs have in a high-rise building up to 60 m high?
question.gold: (a) more than 22 m; (b) at least 1.25 m
rubric: High-rise threshold: uppermost floor more than 22 m above ground on one side
Emergency stair walking width min. 1.25 m (high-rise up to 60 m, at least two stairs in separate fire compartments)
source: High-rise buildings are those intended for long-term human occupation whose upper-most floor on one side of the building is more than 22 m above ground level.
High-rise buildings up to 60 m high: at least two emergency stairs must be available, which must be located opposite in two separate fire compartments. Their walking width must be at least 1.25 m.
context:
Definition of high-rise buildings
High-rise buildings are those intended for long-term human occupation whose upper-most floor on one side of the building is more than 22 m above ground level.

Stairs
High-rise buildings up to 60 m high: at least two emergency stairs must be available, which must be located opposite in two separate fire compartments. Their walking width must be at least 1.25 m. The wellhole must be min. 0.80 m wide in order to avoid having to lay hoses on the stairs. Smoke outlets must be provided at their highest point (5% of the floor area but min. 1 m^2). The exit must be directly into the open air or through a lobby without any fire load. In exceptional cases, one staircase can be approved for high-rise buildings up to 60 m in height, if it is a safety staircase. Requirements for the location of stairs → 2 – 5.

answer.text:
(a) More than **22 m** above ground level.  
(b) Each emergency stair must have a clear walking width of at least **1.25 m**.

question.text: Under German building regulations, (a) what fire resistance class must corridor walls have when they are the side walls of escape routes, and (b) if lighting openings with G-glazing are installed in such walls, what minimum height above floor level must the lower edge of the glass be?

context:
Scope of application
Under building regulations, G-glazing may be installed only where there are no higher requirements for fire protection reasons. A typical area of application for G-glazing is the openings for lighting installed in corridor walls, which have to be constructed fire-retarding (F 30) as the side walls of escape routes. The lower edge of the glass must in this case be at least 1.80 m above floor level, so that in case of fire the corridor remains usable in the radiation shadow.

Construction
Classified materials for the construction of conventional massive load-bearing or non-load-bearing walls are shown in → 8. Steel columns and steel supporting beams are today normally fitted with box-shaped claddings of fire protection boards, whose thickness depends on the profile dimensions and the required fire resistance class → 1 – 3. There are also non-foaming coatings (to F 90) and composite constructions with concrete filling, if necessary with additional reinforcement (F 60). Non-load-bearing separating walls can be constructed as stud partitions of various qualities → 4 – 6.

Corridor walls forming the sides of escape routes must be F 30, and the lower edge of G-glazing must be at least 1.80 m above floor level.

question.text: Under German building regulations, (a) what fire resistance class must corridor walls have when they are the side walls of escape routes, and (b) if lighting openings with G-glazing are installed in such walls, what minimum height above floor level must the lower edge of the glass be?

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: To avoid condensation within a building element, on which side must the vapour barrier be installed?

More recent building ('warm roof', 'warm façade') features an external vapour barrier layer (e.g. waterproofing) and, on account of this, an additional internal vapour barrier. source: Thermal resistance R, unit m^2K/W [m^2hK/kcal] is a property of a layer: R = d/λ (d = layer thickness in m).

context: Thermal resistance R, unit m^2K/W [m^2hK/kcal] is a property of a layer: R = d/λ (d = layer thickness in m). The calculation of the thermal resistance is important for the determination of the heat transfer coefficient U → ③ – ④.

Overall resistance 1/U, unit m^2K/W [m^2hK/kcal], is the sum of the resistances of a building element to the transmission of heat (thermal resistances and surface resistances): 1/U = R_{si} + R + R_{se}

But in example → ⑤ condensation is formed on the inner face of the building element, because the proportion of the surface air film is too large. The surface air film cannot exceed a certain proportion X of the overall resistance 1/U → ③.

answer.text:
For a uniform layer, its thermal resistance is **\(R = d/\lambda\)**, where \(d\) is thickness in metres and \(\lambda\) is the design thermal conductivity in W/(m·K). The unit of \(R\) is m²·K/W.

For the whole element, **\(1/U = R_{si} + \sum R_i + R_{se}\)**: add the internal and external surface resistances to the resistances of all layers (and any applicable air spaces). Thus \(U\) is in W/(m²·K).

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For separating walls between residential or commercial units, what fire resistance duration is required and how far up must the walls extend?

The fire resistance duration of separating walls between residential or commercial units (or units and rooms used otherwise) must correspond to the quality of the load-bearing components of the storey. question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For sound insulation, party walls between flats or houses should always have a mass per unit area of at least how much?
question.gold: 400 kg/m²
source: for this reason, party walls between flats or houses should always weigh at least 400 kg/m².
context: Secondary path transmission reduces the effectiveness of airborne sound insulation more than that of impact sound insulation. For this reason, test certificates for sound-insulated walls should always include the consideration of secondary paths normal in a building. Particularly effective as secondary paths are panels which bend stiffly and have a density of 10–160 kg/m²; for this reason, party walls between flats or houses should always weigh at least 400 kg/m².

Party walls
The diagram → 1 shows a two-skin party wall with a separating joint over the entire depth of the houses. The mass per unit area of the individual layers with plaster must be at least 150 kg/m^2, and the thickness of the separating joint must be at least 30 mm. With a thickness of the separating joint (layer spacing) of more than 50 mm, the mass of each skin can be 100 kg/m^2. The joint cavity is to be filled with gapless full-surface fibre insulating boards, as in DIN 18165 (impact sound insulation boards or separating joint boards approved for this application) without sound bridges.

answer.text: At least **400 kg/m²**.

question.text: Under German building regulations, what are the minimum floor area, minimum ceiling height, and minimum window area (relative to room area) of a residential (habitable) room?

context:
Requirements
Student flats are 'living places' and not considered as residential homes in the sense of the building regulations. The general requirements of the building regulations essentially concern residential rooms with minimum requirements for floor area (8 m^2), ceiling height (2.40 m), orientation, ventilation and lighting (window area 1/8 of the room area), accessibility requirements (i.e. for disabled people) and escape routes (two independent escape routes from each floor, one of which is a legally essential stairway). The state guidelines for student residences set recommended dimensions for living places (approx. 12 m^2 for single rooms and approx. 16 m^2 for flats). In addition to this, a certain area will be required for communal use.

The commonly cited minimums are 8 m² of floor area, 2.40 m ceiling height, and window area equal to at least 1/8 of the room’s floor area.

Ceilings must be fireproof, or at least fire-retarding, and slabs over cellars must be fireproof. Openings in ceilings and floor slabs for which a fire resistance duration is necessary are prohibited. If openings are required, they must be fitted with fire protection closures (doors, etc.) constructed with a fire resistance duration corresponding to that of the slab.
Exceptions apply for buildings of classes 1 and 2, slabs and ceilings above roof spaces, and balconies, slabs and ceilings within residential dwellings.

Solid slabs (e.g. reinforced concrete slabs → ①, hollow pot floors) have sufficient fire resistance under certain conditions without additional protection measures. Numerous construction types are classified in DIN 4102 → ③. Floors consisting of timber joists, steel joists or concrete slabs on profiled metal decking must be protected against fire from below (suspended ceiling → ⑤) and above (covering, screed), in which case the connections at walls and any inserts in the floor have to be taken into account. The fire resistance achieved is normally verified with a test certificate → p. 512. In this case, the entire construction is included in the evaluation. Also usual is the installation of self-supporting suspended ceilings with their own fire resistance class (e.g. to protect the installations in the ceiling void).

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In the grouped room floor plan for apartments (developed in the early 20th century), into which two room groups is the dwelling divided, and which rooms belong to each?
options: Day area (living room, bedrooms) and service area (kitchen, bathrooms)

source: the separation of areas inside the apartment into two 'room groups': the living areas (living room, kitchen and dining area) and the sleeping area (bedrooms and bathrooms)
context:
Grouped room floor plan → ②
The idea of the grouped room floor plan developed at the start of the 20th century and is based on the separation of areas inside the apartment into two 'room groups': the living areas (living room, kitchen and dining area) and the sleeping area (bedrooms and bathrooms).

Central corridor plan → ①
The central corridor plan is the classic floor plan of late 19th-century urban apartment blocks. The rooms are arranged along the two façades and are separated by the (load-bearing) middle wall and the central corridor parallel to it. All rooms can be accessed and used separately. Common and individual areas can be arranged on opposing sides of the façade and related to the particular qualities of the specific side of the building.

question.text: Under German building regulations, what are the minimum floor area, minimum ceiling height, and minimum window area (relative to room area) of a residential (habitable) room?
question.gold: 8 m²; 2.40 m; window area 1/8 of room area
source: minimum requirements for floor area (8 m^2), ceiling height (2.40 m), orientation, ventilation and lighting (window area 1/8 of the room area)
context:
Requirements
Student flats are 'living places' and not considered as residential homes in the sense of the building regulations. The general requirements of the building regulations essentially concern residential rooms with minimum requirements for floor area (8 m^2), ceiling height (2.40 m), orientation, ventilation and lighting (window area 1/8 of the room area), accessibility requirements (i.e. for disabled people) and escape routes (two independent escape routes from each floor, one of which is a legally essential stairway). The state guidelines for student residences set recommended dimensions for living places (approx. 12 m^2 for single rooms and approx. 16 m^2 for flats). In addition to this, a certain area will be required for communal use.

answer.text: Commonly cited values are **8 m²** floor area, **2.40 m** clear ceiling height, and window openings of at least **1/8 (12.5%)** of the room’s net floor area. **Caveat:** German building rules are state-specific, and there is no uniform nationwide minimum floor area; 2.40 m also has exceptions in some states or building types.
