question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: When should the entrance hall of a dwelling be enclosed with an inner door to act as a wind lobby, and in which case is this unnecessary?

A stair shaft can provide the wind protection instead
source: if the entrance is into a stair shaft, then this can provide wind protection

context:
Entrance
The entrance is the face of a house, where visitors gain their first impression. A multitude of functions have to be practically arranged and appropriately designed → ①. If the entrance is into the open air, it should be protected from the prevailing wind direction if possible. If weather conditions are unfavourable, a lobby is also recommended to prevent wind blowing through → p. 136 (if the entrance is into a stair shaft, then this can provide wind protection).

Entrance hall
The entrance hall should be enclosed where the entrance leads directly to the open air with an inner door (wind lobby function). It should also offer sufficient room for a lot of moving around → ④. This is where reception, greeting, taking off and putting on coats, and taking leave all take place, but also offers the first orientation for the visitor → ① – ③. Countless objects therefore have to be arranged practically yet tidily in this limited space → ⑤, ⑥. The most important communal areas like the kitchen, WC and staircase should be directly accessible from the entrance hall.

Entrance
The entrance is the face of a house, where visitors gain their first impression. A multitude of functions have to be practically arranged and appropriately designed → ①. If the entrance is into the open air, it should be protected from the prevailing wind direction if possible. If weather conditions are unfavourable, a lobby is also recommended to prevent wind blowing through → p. 136 (if the entrance is into a stair shaft, then this can provide wind protection).

answer.text: Provide an inner door to form a wind lobby when the dwelling’s entrance opens directly to the outside. It is generally unnecessary when the entrance is reached from an enclosed, sheltered common stairwell or corridor.

context:
Grouped room floor plan → ②
The idea of the grouped room floor plan developed at the start of the 20th century and is based on the separation of areas inside the apartment into two 'room groups': the living areas (living room, kitchen and dining area) and the sleeping area (bedrooms and bathrooms).

Central corridor plan → ①
The central corridor plan is the classic floor plan of late 19th-century urban apartment blocks. The rooms are arranged along the two façades and are separated by the (load-bearing) middle wall and the central corridor parallel to it. All rooms can be accessed and used separately. Common and individual areas can be arranged on opposing sides of the façade and related to the particular qualities of the specific side of the building.

context:
Communal storerooms
In addition to the storerooms or storage spaces in each flat, for residential buildings in building classes 3–5, the building regulations require an easily accessible (communal) storeroom for prams, pushchairs and bicycles. Corresponding areas should also be provided in other residential buildings and detached houses.

Solid waste can be temporarily stored inside the building. Waste can be stored temporarily inside buildings with more than two flats or a usable area of 400 m² (building classes 3–5) only if the rubbish collection room complies with the following requirements:

For the design of these rooms, it can be assumed that at least one vehicle per occupant (including children) has to be accommodated. In addition to bicycles, prams and pushchairs, it is also necessary to consider mopeds, tricycles, trailers etc. → ①.

The rooms should if possible be located at street level, be lockable and equipped with hooks and bicycle stands to secure the stored vehicles. question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In office planning, which grid module dimensions have proved successful in recent years for (a) single-room offices and (b) office types based on the combi principle?
source: The modular dimensions, which have proved successful in recent years, are 1.50 m for single-room offices and 1.35 m for office types based on the combi principle.
context: Grid module spacings define possible room sizes through the resulting spacing of columns and façades. The fitting out and façade grids must be the same in order to enable the partitions to connect to the windows. The structural grid can be offset against the fitting out grid. This reduces the problem of connecting the partitions to columns, but loses space in the rooms, which contain columns. Because of the different lifecycles of the building elements, an adaptable module dimension should be chosen. The modular dimensions, which have proved successful in recent years, are 1.50 m for single-room offices and 1.35 m for office types based on the combi principle.

Modular dimension 1.50 m
This is the economical module dimension for single-room offices consisting mainly of double workstations. Workstation depth 2.20 m (80 cm desk, 1 m movement area, 40 cm shelf behind). With 10 cm wall thickness, this gives 4.40 m clear room space.
The usual depth of buildings with central corridors is 12–13 m. This dimension is only of limited practicality for combi-offices.

Modular dimension 1.50 m

The usual depth of buildings with central corridors is 12–13 m. This dimension is only of limited practicality for combi-offices.

Modular dimension 1.35 m
Room widths of 3.80 m (~18 m^2 usable area) enable:
– additional filing storage; two computer workstations with a depth of 0.90 m, as recommended by accident insurance companies; one drawing board or drawing machine and one desk; one desk and meeting table for four people. All usual office workstations are possible, offering high flexibility of use without moving the partitions.

question.text: To which compass orientation should a bathroom in a dwelling be oriented, and if natural ventilation and lighting are not possible, according to which German standard must effective mechanical ventilation be provided?
question.gold: North; DIN 18017-3
source: The bathroom should be oriented to the north, and if possible have natural ventilation and lighting (otherwise provide effective mechanical ventilation according to DIN 18017-3).
context: A bathroom is defined as an independent room with bath/shower and toilet and, according to building regulations, belongs to the minimum equipment of a flat or house. In larger houses, bath and WC should be in separate rooms, or an additional WC (guest WC) should be provided. The bathroom should be oriented to the north, and if possible have natural ventilation and lighting (otherwise provide effective mechanical ventilation according to DIN 18017-3). The bathroom is normally next to the bedroom → ⑤ – ⑥, ⑧ – ⑩, although it is also often convenient for technical reasons to place bath and kitchen (or WC and kitchen) on a common installation shaft → ⑧ – ⑨.

Central function zone → ③
In buildings of greater depth, the central area of the flat can be widened to form a zone of subsidiary space and the façades can be completely used for living areas. Bathrooms with artificial lighting (or lit indirectly from other areas of the flat), kitchens, cupboard and storage areas can be placed here, and appropriate passages and spaces provide the connection to the outside rooms.

meta.title: 卫生间朝向、采光与通风

answer.text: A bathroom is preferably oriented east for morning daylight. If natural ventilation is not possible, effective mechanical ventilation must comply with **DIN 18017-3**.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Approximately how many workstations does a group office have, and how many workstations characterise the large-scale open-plan office landscapes made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation?
source: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations
The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department.
Large-scale office landscapes with 100 or more workstations are made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation
context:
Group office: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department. This arrangement is preferred above all for creative, design or coordination and development activities with high internal communication needs.
→ 2

Group office: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department. This arrangement is preferred above all for creative, design or coordination and development activities with high internal communication needs.
→ 2

Open-plan office: A form of office developed in the 1960s and 1970s of the last century. Large-scale office landscapes with 100 or more workstations are made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation; they stand for free communication and openness. Economical cubic structures, however, have the disadvantage of high maintenance costs. This form is not very popular among users → 3.

Single-room offices are suitable for independent or concentrated work, as a single-person room or for a few people in very small groups who need to exchange information constantly. This arrangement has been common in Germany since World War II and still has its justification when the requirements of the workplace correspond (→ Gruner, Jahr; Steidle, Kissler; or → new offices for the Federal Environment Office, Dessau, Sauerbruch, Hutton) or in newbuild high-rise offices, where the structure of the building can be so decisive that it leads to the very standardised character of spatial and organisational working practices.

A more sensitive relationship to the direct working environment is closely linked to the predominant value orientation in the company. This is reflected in the attitude to the quality of the workplace (daylight, environmental context, energy consumption), and the activity (ecological viewpoints, material use, waste disposal). The workplace is an important place for social interaction among the users, which is increasing in relevance due to formalised work structures (IT, work organisation etc.). Increased mental and physical stress leads to a greater awareness of the working environment (sufficient space, some personal choice in furnishings, ventilation, lighting, sufficient protection from disruptions). 75% of daily work takes place at the 'close and extended workplace' → ②. Necessary work contacts and collectively used facilities are significant, thus the requirement for a mixed provision of single and group rooms, 'personal' and 'collective' workplaces → ③ – ④. In addition to the refurbishment of existing office space, new spatial concepts involving single and group rooms are starting to appear (Fuchs, Gottschalk, Henkel → refs).

answer.text: Answer: D

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Approximately how many workstations does a group office have, and how many workstations characterise the large-scale open-plan office landscapes made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation?
question.gold: Group office approx. 4–16 workstations; open-plan 100 or more
source: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations
The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department.
Large-scale office landscapes with 100 or more workstations are made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation
context:
Group office: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department. This arrangement is preferred above all for creative, design or coordination and development activities with high internal communication needs.
→ 2

Group office: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department. This arrangement is preferred above all for creative, design or coordination and development activities with high internal communication needs.
→ 2

Open-plan office: A form of office developed in the 1960s and 1970s of the last century. Large-scale office landscapes with 100 or more workstations are made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation; they stand for free communication and openness. Economical cubic structures, however, have the disadvantage of high maintenance costs. This form is not very popular among users → 3.

Single-room offices are suitable for independent or concentrated work, as a single-person room or for a few people in very small groups who need to exchange information constantly. This arrangement has been common in Germany since World War II and still has its justification when the requirements of the workplace correspond (→ Gruner, Jahr; Steidle, Kissler; or → new offices for the Federal Environment Office, Dessau, Sauerbruch, Hutton) or in newbuild high-rise offices, where the structure of the building can be so decisive that it leads to the very standardised character of spatial and organisational working practices.

A more sensitive relationship to the direct working environment is closely linked to the predominant value orientation in the company. This is reflected in the attitude to the quality of the workplace (daylight, environmental context, energy consumption), and the activity (ecological viewpoints, material use, waste disposal). The workplace is an important place for social interaction among the users, which is increasing in relevance due to formalised work structures (IT, work organisation etc.). Increased mental and physical stress leads to a greater awareness of the working environment (sufficient space, some personal choice in furnishings, ventilation, lighting, sufficient protection from disruptions). 75% of daily work takes place at the 'close and extended workplace' → ②. Necessary work contacts and collectively used facilities are significant, thus the requirement for a mixed provision of single and group rooms, 'personal' and 'collective' workplaces → ③ – ④. In addition to the refurbishment of existing office space, new spatial concepts involving single and group rooms are starting to appear (Fuchs, Gottschalk, Henkel → refs).

answer.text: A group office typically has about **3–25 workstations**. Large open-plan office landscapes may have roughly **100–1,000 workstations**.

source: The modular dimensions, which have proved successful in recent years, are 1.50 m for single-room offices and 1.35 m for office types based on the combi principle.
context: Grid module spacings define possible room sizes through the resulting spacing of columns and façades. The fitting out and façade grids must be the same in order to enable the partitions to connect to the windows. The structural grid can be offset against the fitting out grid. This reduces the problem of connecting the partitions to columns, but loses space in the rooms, which contain columns. Because of the different lifecycles of the building elements, an adaptable module dimension should be chosen. Communal storerooms
In addition to the storerooms or storage spaces in each flat, for residential buildings in building classes 3–5, the building regulations require an easily accessible (communal) storeroom for prams, pushchairs and bicycles. Corresponding areas should also be provided in other residential buildings and detached houses.

Solid waste can be temporarily stored inside the building. Waste can be stored temporarily inside buildings with more than two flats or a usable area of 400 m² (building classes 3–5) only if the rubbish collection room complies with the following requirements:

For the design of these rooms, it can be assumed that at least one vehicle per occupant (including children) has to be accommodated. In addition to bicycles, prams and pushchairs, it is also necessary to consider mopeds, tricycles, trailers etc. → ①.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Group rooms (smaller open-plan offices for work groups with constant information exchange) limit the size of the workplace surroundings. What is the guideline maximum distance from a workplace to a window for them?
question.gold: max. 7.5 m
source: via the size of the workplace surroundings (max. 7.5 m to a window)
context: Group rooms (smaller open-plan) are suitable for work groups with constant information exchange. This form of office was an attempt to install room layouts with more scope for individual decisions (→ Changes at the workplace, p. 232 ), via the size of the workplace surroundings (max. 7.5 m to a window), and thus improve the working conditions of an open-plan arrangement (light, air, individuality), which were found to be inadequate with the increasing demands on office work. It is possible to do without full air conditioning in favour of back-up ventilation services, in addition to opening windows and using radiators.

question.text: According to the German high-rise building regulations: (a) above what height of the uppermost floor (on one side of the building, above ground level) does a building intended for long-term human occupation count as a high-rise building, and (b) what minimum walking width must each of the emergency stairs have in a high-rise building up to 60 m high?
source: High-rise buildings are those intended for long-term human occupation whose upper-most floor on one side of the building is more than 22 m above ground level.
High-rise buildings up to 60 m high: at least two emergency stairs must be available, which must be located opposite in two separate fire compartments. Their walking width must be at least 1.25 m.
context:
Definition of high-rise buildings
High-rise buildings are those intended for long-term human occupation whose upper-most floor on one side of the building is more than 22 m above ground level.

Stairs
High-rise buildings up to 60 m high: at least two emergency stairs must be available, which must be located opposite in two separate fire compartments. Their walking width must be at least 1.25 m. The wellhole must be min. 0.80 m wide in order to avoid having to lay hoses on the stairs. Smoke outlets must be provided at their highest point (5% of the floor area but min. 1 m^2). The exit must be directly into the open air or through a lobby without any fire load. In exceptional cases, one staircase can be approved for high-rise buildings up to 60 m in height, if it is a safety staircase. Requirements for the location of stairs → 2 – 5.

answer.text: Answer: B

question.text: In German (DIN-based) planning guidance on parking for private houses, which form of car shelter (other than an enclosed garage) is described as cheaper, more beneficial in terms of building physics because it avoids condensation in cold cars in winter, and space-saving?

context: Space requirement → 7 – 12. A reduction in the parking area is possible for private houses. The tendency of modern cars to get larger (including in height) should be taken into account.

In addition to garages, roofed-over parking places (carports) represent a cheaper, more beneficial in terms of building physics (no condensation in cold cars in the winter!) and space-saving possibility for protecting cars adequately from the weather (a close wall on the weather side is a good idea). A combination with enclosed storerooms (for bicycles etc.) is to be recommended → 11. Carports are particularly suitable for communal parking places → 12.

answer.text:
An open carport allows continuous air circulation, which prevents moisture build-up and condensation on cold, wet cars in winter (reducing rust), while also being significantly cheaper and less space-demanding to construct than enclosed garage structures.

question.text: Under German building regulations, (a) what fire resistance class must corridor walls have when they are the side walls of escape routes, and (b) if lighting openings with G-glazing are installed in such walls, what minimum height above floor level must the lower edge of the glass be?
source: A typical area of application for G-glazing is the openings for lighting installed in corridor walls, which have to be constructed fire-retarding (F 30) as the side walls of escape routes.
context:
Scope of application
Under building regulations, G-glazing may be installed only where there are no higher requirements for fire protection reasons. A typical area of application for G-glazing is the openings for lighting installed in corridor walls, which have to be constructed fire-retarding (F 30) as the side walls of escape routes. The lower edge of the glass must in this case be at least 1.80 m above floor level, so that in case of fire the corridor remains usable in the radiation shadow.

Construction
Classified materials for the construction of conventional massive load-bearing or non-load-bearing walls are shown in → 8. Steel columns and steel supporting beams are today normally fitted with box-shaped claddings of fire protection boards, whose thickness depends on the profile dimensions and the required fire resistance class → 1 – 3. There are also non-foaming coatings (to F 90) and composite constructions with concrete filling, if necessary with additional reinforcement (F 60). Non-load-bearing separating walls can be constructed as stud partitions of various qualities → 4 – 6.

answer.text:
Answering the question based on German building regulations (Musterbauordnung – MBO § 36):

1. Walls of necessary corridors (escape routes) are generally required to be fire-retardant (*feuerhemmend*, corresponding to fire resistance class **F 30**).
2. Openings with G-class glazing (which only prevents the passage of flames and smoke but does not block heat radiation) are permitted only if the lower edge of the glazing is at least **1.80 m** above floor level to protect escaping persons from radiant heat.

Answer: A

question.text: For escape routes in high-rise buildings under German regulations, what are (a) the minimum width of escape routes, (b) the maximum walking distance from any point in an occupied room, and (c) the maximum length of a branch corridor with only one escape direction when no second escape route is available?
rubric: Dead-end corridor max. 10 m (20 m only with a second escape route)
source: Escape routes are min. 1.25 m wide and should if possible lead in two directions, to each staircase. The maximum walking distance from each point of an occupied room may not exceed 25 m. Corridors with two escape directions may be max. 40 m long. After 20 m, a smoke-proof self-closing door must be installed. Branch corridors with only one escape direction may be max. 10 m long. If a second escape route (e.g. an escape balcony) is available, max. 20 m.
context:
Escape routes
Escape routes are min. 1.25 m wide and should if possible lead in two directions, to each staircase. The maximum walking distance from each point of an occupied room may not exceed 25 m. Corridors with two escape directions may be max. 40 m long. After 20 m, a smoke-proof self-closing door must be installed. Branch corridors with only one escape direction may be max. 10 m long. If a second escape route (e.g. an escape balcony) is available, max. 20 m.

answer.text:
Under German building regulations for high-rise buildings (*Muster-Hochhaus-Richtlinie* – MHHR):

* **(a) Minimum clear width of escape routes:** **1.20 m** (for necessary corridors and stairways)
* **(b) Maximum walking distance:** **35 m** (actual walking distance / *Lauflänge* from any point in an occupied room to a safety stairwell exit)
* **(c) Maximum length of a branch/dead-end corridor (*Stichflur*):** **10 m** (or up to **15 m** where the general *Musterbauordnung* baseline applies)

options: Movable systems to shade the low sun
A slight fixed roof overhang is sufficient

Systems

South windows need effective shading above all in the early year and autumn, with low sun. In the high summer, slight roof overhangs are sufficient to avoid direct sunshine.

answer.text:
In German building practice (e.g., DIN 4108-2 for summer thermal protection), east- and west-facing facades receive direct solar radiation at low sun angles. question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Single-leaf external masonry walls without an additional insulation layer must meet high thermal insulation requirements. What materials does this restrict their construction to?
options: Highly insulating blocks (e.g. aerated blocks) with special thermally insulating mortar and plaster
Dense solid clay bricks with standard mortar and lime plaster
Any masonry unit, provided a mesh-reinforced render is applied
source: Single-leaf external walls → ① – ② are unproblematic regarding building physics, but on account of the high thermal insulation requirements can only be built with materials with high thermal insulation value (e.g. aerated blocks) and special thermally insulated mortars and plasters.
Single-leaf walls with additional insulation layers → ③ – ⑥ (external, internal insulation → Building physics, p. 471 ff.) are therefore a common alternative.
context:
External wall construction
Single-leaf external walls → ① – ② are unproblematic regarding building physics, but on account of the high thermal insulation requirements can only be built with materials with high thermal insulation value (e.g. aerated blocks) and special thermally insulated mortars and plasters. If the blocks used are susceptible to frost damage, they have to be rendered or protected in other ways. If the masonry is externally visible, then each course must consist of at least two rows of blocks of the same height with a continuous 20 mm thick longitudinal joint between them, and each course staggered and mortared without voids.
Single-leaf walls with additional insulation layers → ③ – ⑥ (external, internal insulation → Building physics, p. 471 ff.) are therefore a common alternative.

On the external side of the insulating layers, there is a risk of cracking due to heat build-up and substrate with poor shear strength, so mineral render reinforced with mesh is used here (or plastic modified render).

answer.text:
* **Thermal resistance of a single layer ($R$):** 
  $R = \frac{d}{\lambda} \quad [\text{m}^2\text{K/W}]$ 
  *(where $d$ is the layer thickness in meters and $\lambda$ is the design thermal conductivity in $\text{W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$)*

* **Overall thermal resistance ($1/U$ or $R_T$):** 
  $\frac{1}{U} = R_T = R_{si} + \sum R_i + R_{se} \quad [\text{m}^2\text{K/W}]$

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Compared with a poorly insulated building envelope, how severe are the consequences of a thermal bridge in a highly insulated envelope?
options: About the same; insulation level is irrelevant
Negligible once U-values are low enough
Less severe, because overall heat loss is lower
source: Thermal bridges are parts of building elements with low thermal insulation compared with surrounding areas.
Thus it should be borne in mind that this thermal bridging effect can have considerably worse consequences with highly insulated elements than with building elements with less thermal insulation.
context:
Thermal bridge
Thermal bridges are parts of building elements with low thermal insulation compared with surrounding areas. This results in the proportion of the surface air film in the overall resistance increasing so that the surface temperature of the inner side of the thermal bridge sinks and condensation forms.

Good thermal insulation includes not only highly insulated building components, but also the appropriate connections between the building elements. There is a danger of additional heat loss at these joints and low surface temperature in the building elements during the heating period. Additional consumption of energy for heating and the possibility of condensation and mould formation are the result. Thus it should be borne in mind that this thermal bridging effect can have considerably worse consequences with highly insulated elements than with building elements with less thermal insulation. Thermal bridges can be considered, according to EnEV, for the determination of the annual heating energy demand by increasing the thermal transmission values (U-values) or in a separate verification.

Thus it should be borne in mind that this thermal bridging effect can have considerably worse consequences with highly insulated elements than with building elements with less thermal insulation. answer.text:
In German building physics and design standards (such as DIN 4108), as the standard of thermal insulation increases, the relative proportion of heat lost via thermal bridges increases significantly (potentially accounting for up to 30–50% of transmission heat losses). Furthermore, because modern insulated buildings are much more airtight, the risk of localized condensation and mold growth at thermal bridges is considerably higher. Therefore, the consequences of a thermal bridge are considered considerably worse in a highly insulated envelope.

answer.text:
In a highly insulated envelope, the consequences of a thermal bridge are **significantly more severe**:

1. **Relative heat loss:** Thermal bridges can account for up to **30% to 50%** of total transmission heat losses (compared to a negligible fraction in poorly insulated envelopes).
2. **Moisture and mold risk:** The steep temperature gradient between the warm, well-insulated surfaces and the uninsulated bridge drastically lowers the interior surface temperature at that point, creating a critical risk of condensation and mold growth (failing the DIN 4108-2 requirement of $f_{Rsi} \ge 0.70$).

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: To avoid condensation within a building element, on which side must the vapour barrier be installed?
options: In the ventilated cavity outside the insulation
In the middle of the insulation layer
source: If there is a vapour barrier on the outside, then the entire vapour pressure gradient occurs there and the result is condensation → 8; if this is to be avoided, then a vapour barrier must be installed on the warm side
context:
Construction with vapour barrier → 3 – 4
More recent building ('warm roof', 'warm façade') features an external vapour barrier layer (e.g. waterproofing) and, on account of this, an additional internal vapour barrier. In order to prevent condensation on the inside face of the building element, the layers in front of the vapour barrier cannot exceed a certain proportion of the overall thermal resistance → p. 472. Warm façades require careful construction and have therefore mostly become established as prefabricated systems (sandwich construction). In a warm roof, a water vapour pressure equalisation layer is arranged under the waterproofing, and only an equalisation layer for the damping of stresses is provided under the vapour barrier.

Vapour barrier at the correct location
If there is a vapour barrier on the outside, then the entire vapour pressure gradient occurs there and the result is condensation → 8; if this is to be avoided, then a vapour barrier must be installed on the warm side with an equivalent diffusion resistance suitable for the location, in which case the layers in front of the vapour barrier must not exceed a certain proportion of the overall thermal resistance 1/U → 9.

The vapour barrier is under the thermal insulation to prevent condensation inside the roof construction. When the vapour barrier is installed, it is important that all air flow between interior and roof construction is prevented. Any penetration points, laps and junctions with building elements must be carefully sealed. Inner cladding is normally plasterboard on support construction (pay attention to the possibility of cracks!).

answer.text:
To prevent water vapour from the interior air diffusing into the thermal insulation layer and condensing as it cools down, standard German building physics practice (e.g., DIN 4108) requires the vapour barrier (Dampfsperre/Dampfbremse) to be placed on the warm (interior) side of the thermal insulation.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Why does the building industry commonly prefer unventilated over ventilated insulated pitched-roof construction?

Thermally insulated roofs can be divided into ventilated and non-ventilated construction. Ceilings must be fireproof, or at least fire-retarding, and slabs over cellars must be fireproof. Openings in ceilings and floor slabs for which a fire resistance duration is necessary are prohibited. If openings are required, they must be fitted with fire protection closures (doors, etc.) constructed with a fire resistance duration corresponding to that of the slab.
Exceptions apply for buildings of classes 1 and 2, slabs and ceilings above roof spaces, and balconies, slabs and ceilings within residential dwellings.

Solid slabs (e.g. reinforced concrete slabs → ①, hollow pot floors) have sufficient fire resistance under certain conditions without additional protection measures. Numerous construction types are classified in DIN 4102 → ③. Floors consisting of timber joists, steel joists or concrete slabs on profiled metal decking must be protected against fire from below (suspended ceiling → ⑤) and above (covering, screed), in which case the connections at walls and any inserts in the floor have to be taken into account. The fire resistance achieved is normally verified with a test certificate → p. 512. In this case, the entire construction is included in the evaluation. Also usual is the installation of self-supporting suspended ceilings with their own fire resistance class (e.g. to protect the installations in the ceiling void).

question.text: Under German building regulations, when a kitchen is a habitable room, what minimum clear ceiling height and what minimum window area (structural dimensions, relative to the net floor area) must it have?
question.gold: 2.40 m; 1/8 of the net floor area
rubric: Window area at least 1/8 of net floor area
source: As a habitable room, the kitchen must have a clear ceiling height of at least 2.40 m and a window area (structural dimensions) of at least 1/8 of the net floor area.
context: Kitchens and kitchenettes without windows are generally undesirable and only permissible if effective ventilation is guaranteed. As a habitable room, the kitchen must have a clear ceiling height of at least 2.40 m and a window area (structural dimensions) of at least 1/8 of the net floor area.

answer.text:
Under the German Model Building Code (*Musterbauordnung* – MBO § 47) and most state regulations (*Landesbauordnungen*):

* **Minimum clear ceiling height:** **2.40 m** (can be reduced to **2.20 m** in attic/top floors (*Dachgeschosse*); some federal states require up to 2.50 m for standard storeys).
* **Minimum window area:** At least **1/8 (12.5%)** of the room’s net floor area, measured as the structural opening dimension (*Rohbaumaß*).

question.text: Under German building regulations, what are the minimum floor area, minimum ceiling height, and minimum window area (relative to room area) of a residential (habitable) room?
question.gold: 8 m²; 2.40 m; window area 1/8 of room area
source: minimum requirements for floor area (8 m^2), ceiling height (2.40 m), orientation, ventilation and lighting (window area 1/8 of the room area)
context:
Requirements
Student flats are 'living places' and not considered as residential homes in the sense of the building regulations. The general requirements of the building regulations essentially concern residential rooms with minimum requirements for floor area (8 m^2), ceiling height (2.40 m), orientation, ventilation and lighting (window area 1/8 of the room area), accessibility requirements (i.e. for disabled people) and escape routes (two independent escape routes from each floor, one of which is a legally essential stairway). The state guidelines for student residences set recommended dimensions for living places (approx. 12 m^2 for single rooms and approx. 16 m^2 for flats). In addition to this, a certain area will be required for communal use.

answer.text:
Under the German Model Building Regulation (*Musterbauordnung* – MBO) and typical state codes:

* **Minimum floor area:** Not specified in the MBO, but individual state building and housing laws (*Wohnungsaufsichtsgesetze*) generally require a minimum of **6 m² to 9 m²** for a habitable room.
* **Minimum ceiling height:** **2.40 m** over at least half of the room's floor area (reduced to **2.20 m** in attics/sloped roofs).
* **Minimum window area:** At least **1/8 (12.5%)** of the room’s net floor area (measured as the structural masonry opening, *Rohbaumaß*).

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For sound protection in dwellings, noisy service elements (water and waste pipes, gas risers, waste disposal units, lifts) may not be installed in the walls of which rooms?

Sound from services can occur as plumbing fixture sound, pipework sound or filling/emptying sounds. The maximum permissible sound level from services in neighbouring residential units is 35 dB (A). question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In the grouped room floor plan for apartments (developed in the early 20th century), into which two room groups is the dwelling divided, and which rooms belong to each?

source: the separation of areas inside the apartment into two 'room groups': the living areas (living room, kitchen and dining area) and the sleeping area (bedrooms and bathrooms)
context:
Grouped room floor plan → ②
The idea of the grouped room floor plan developed at the start of the 20th century and is based on the separation of areas inside the apartment into two 'room groups': the living areas (living room, kitchen and dining area) and the sleeping area (bedrooms and bathrooms).

Central corridor plan → ①
The central corridor plan is the classic floor plan of late 19th-century urban apartment blocks. The rooms are arranged along the two façades and are separated by the (load-bearing) middle wall and the central corridor parallel to it. All rooms can be accessed and used separately. Common and individual areas can be arranged on opposing sides of the façade and related to the particular qualities of the specific side of the building.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In dwelling design, to which compass directions are parents' bedrooms and children's bedrooms normally oriented?
options: Parents: south to west; children: east or southeast
Parents: east or southeast; children: south to west
Parents: west; children: north to east
source: These would normally be aligned to east or southeast (parents) or south to west (children) and separated from the living room in another part of the home.
context: → ② – ③: bedrooms with minimal space of approx. 13 m² (as parents’ room or twin bedroom) and approx. 8 m² (single room). These would normally be aligned to east or southeast (parents) or south to west (children) and separated from the living room in another part of the home.

answer.text:
In German architectural design practice (as outlined in reference works such as Neufert's *Bauentwurfslehre*):

- **Parents' bedrooms** are typically oriented toward the **east or southeast** to receive morning sunlight while remaining cooler in the evening.
- **Children's bedrooms** (which also function as play- and workrooms throughout the afternoon) are typically oriented toward the **south to west** to maximize daylight during the day and late afternoon.

Answer: B

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In a house, which of the most important communal areas should be directly accessible from the entrance hall?

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: What building-services provision do open kitchens (kitchens open to the living/dining space of a dwelling) require, and for what reason?
question.gold: Good ventilation and extraction, so cooking smells do not impair the living and dining areas

effective air extraction/ventilation against cooking smells
rubric: Purpose: avoid cooking smells in living/dining areas
source: Open kitchens require good ventilation and extraction in order not to impair the living and dining room areas with cooking smells.
context: Modern kitchen designs are moving away from the fitted kitchen. The kitchen area is seen as an ensemble of independent objects developed in each case from formal and functional conditions, which are grouped like pieces of furniture in an (ideally generous) residential room. Open kitchens require good ventilation and extraction in order not to impair the living and dining room areas with cooking smells. In many cases, a mobile divider is to be recommended, for example using a curtain → 9.

answer.text:
Under German building regulations and standards (DIN 1946-6 / DIN 18017-3):

* **Provision:** Open kitchens require **mechanical exhaust air extraction** (an exhaust air outlet / *Abluftelement* or mechanical ventilation system) located directly in the cooking zone, typically designed for an exhaust volume flow rate of at least **45 to 60 m³/h** (boost mode up to 100+ m³/h). 
* **Reason:** Because open kitchens share air volume with the living/dining space (which functions as a supply-air or overflow zone), mechanical extraction establishes a continuous negative pressure gradient toward the cooking area to prevent cooking odors, aerosolized grease, and high moisture loads from dispersing into the living space and causing indoor air degradation or mold growth.

*(Note: If a room-air-dependent fireplace/stove is also present in the shared space, a **window contact switch** or differential pressure monitor is additionally required by MBO/FeuVO to prevent deadly flue gas backdraft).*

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In office planning, which grid module dimensions have proved successful in recent years for (a) single-room offices and (b) office types based on the combi principle?
source: The modular dimensions, which have proved successful in recent years, are 1.50 m for single-room offices and 1.35 m for office types based on the combi principle.
context: Grid module spacings define possible room sizes through the resulting spacing of columns and façades. The fitting out and façade grids must be the same in order to enable the partitions to connect to the windows. The structural grid can be offset against the fitting out grid. This reduces the problem of connecting the partitions to columns, but loses space in the rooms, which contain columns. Because of the different lifecycles of the building elements, an adaptable module dimension should be chosen. The modular dimensions, which have proved successful in recent years, are 1.50 m for single-room offices and 1.35 m for office types based on the combi principle.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Approximately how many workstations does a group office have, and how many workstations characterise the large-scale open-plan office landscapes made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation?

source: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations
The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department.
Large-scale office landscapes with 100 or more workstations are made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation
context:
Group office: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department. This arrangement is preferred above all for creative, design or coordination and development activities with high internal communication needs.
→ 2

Group office: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department. This arrangement is preferred above all for creative, design or coordination and development activities with high internal communication needs.
→ 2

Open-plan office: A form of office developed in the 1960s and 1970s of the last century. Large-scale office landscapes with 100 or more workstations are made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation; they stand for free communication and openness. Economical cubic structures, however, have the disadvantage of high maintenance costs. This form is not very popular among users → 3.

Single-room offices are suitable for independent or concentrated work, as a single-person room or for a few people in very small groups who need to exchange information constantly. This arrangement has been common in Germany since World War II and still has its justification when the requirements of the workplace correspond (→ Gruner, Jahr; Steidle, Kissler; or → new offices for the Federal Environment Office, Dessau, Sauerbruch, Hutton) or in newbuild high-rise offices, where the structure of the building can be so decisive that it leads to the very standardised character of spatial and organisational working practices.

A more sensitive relationship to the direct working environment is closely linked to the predominant value orientation in the company. This is reflected in the attitude to the quality of the workplace (daylight, environmental context, energy consumption), and the activity (ecological viewpoints, material use, waste disposal). The workplace is an important place for social interaction among the users, which is increasing in relevance due to formalised work structures (IT, work organisation etc.). Increased mental and physical stress leads to a greater awareness of the working environment (sufficient space, some personal choice in furnishings, ventilation, lighting, sufficient protection from disruptions). 75% of daily work takes place at the 'close and extended workplace' → ②. Necessary work contacts and collectively used facilities are significant, thus the requirement for a mixed provision of single and group rooms, 'personal' and 'collective' workplaces → ③ – ④. In addition to the refurbishment of existing office space, new spatial concepts involving single and group rooms are starting to appear (Fuchs, Gottschalk, Henkel → refs).

answer.text:
* **Group office (*Gruppenbüro*):** Approximately **8 to 20 (up to 25)** workstations.
* **Large-scale open-plan office (*Großraumbüro* / *Bürolandschaft*):** Typically **50 or more** workstations (often ranging from 50 to several hundred, generally covering at least 400 m²).

Economical cubic structures, however, have the disadvantage of high maintenance costs. This form is not very popular among users → 3.

Single-room offices are suitable for independent or concentrated work, as a single-person room or for a few people in very small groups who need to exchange information constantly. This arrangement has been common in Germany since World War II and still has its justification when the requirements of the workplace correspond (→ Gruner, Jahr; Steidle, Kissler; or → new offices for the Federal Environment Office, Dessau, Sauerbruch, Hutton) or in newbuild high-rise offices, where the structure of the building can be so decisive that it leads to the very standardised character of spatial and organisational working practices.

A more sensitive relationship to the direct working environment is closely linked to the predominant value orientation in the company. This is reflected in the attitude to the quality of the workplace (daylight, environmental context, energy consumption), and the activity (ecological viewpoints, material use, waste disposal). The workplace is an important place for social interaction among the users, which is increasing in relevance due to formalised work structures (IT, work organisation etc.). Increased mental and physical stress leads to a greater awareness of the working environment (sufficient space, some personal choice in furnishings, ventilation, lighting, sufficient protection from disruptions). 75% of daily work takes place at the 'close and extended workplace' → ②. Necessary work contacts and collectively used facilities are significant, thus the requirement for a mixed provision of single and group rooms, 'personal' and 'collective' workplaces → ③ – ④. In addition to the refurbishment of existing office space, new spatial concepts involving single and group rooms are starting to appear (Fuchs, Gottschalk, Henkel → refs).

answer.text:
Based on standard German architectural design references (such as *Neufert Architects' Data*):

* **Group offices (*Gruppenbüro*)** typically accommodate **4–16 workstations**.
* **Open-plan office landscapes (*Bürolandschaften*)**, developed for deep floor-plate buildings requiring artificial lighting and mechanical ventilation, typically encompass **100 or more workstations** (often spanning 1,000 m² or more).

Answer: A

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In office planning, which grid module dimensions have proved successful in recent years for (a) single-room offices and (b) office types based on the combi principle?

context: Grid module spacings define possible room sizes through the resulting spacing of columns and façades. Stairs
High-rise buildings up to 60 m high: at least two emergency stairs must be available, which must be located opposite in two separate fire compartments. Their walking width must be at least 1.25 m. The wellhole must be min. 0.80 m wide in order to avoid having to lay hoses on the stairs. Smoke outlets must be provided at their highest point (5% of the floor area but min. 1 m^2). The exit must be directly into the open air or through a lobby without any fire load. In exceptional cases, one staircase can be approved for high-rise buildings up to 60 m in height, if it is a safety staircase. Requirements for the location of stairs → 2 – 5.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For a comfortable stair with the lowest energy requirement, a standard design rule combines riser height r and tread depth t, based on the stride length of an adult. Within what range should 2r + t lie?
source: In order to determine a suitable pitch with the lowest energy requirement, this formula applies: 2 r + t = 59–65 cm.
context: The experience of using stairs and access routes is very varied: from the creative possibilities of the most diverse residential stairs to an elaborate outside staircase, which one can stride up and down. Climbing stairs takes on average seven times the energy input as walking on the flat. From the physiological point of view, the best use of 'climbing effort' is at a stair pitch of 30° and a ratio of riser (r) to tread (t) of 17/29. The pitch is determined by the stride length of an adult (approx. 59–65 cm). In order to determine a suitable pitch with the lowest energy requirement, this formula applies: 2 r + t = 59–65 cm.

question.text: Under German building regulations, (a) what fire resistance class must corridor walls have when they are the side walls of escape routes, and (b) if lighting openings with G-glazing are installed in such walls, what minimum height above floor level must the lower edge of the glass be?

context:
Scope of application
Under building regulations, G-glazing may be installed only where there are no higher requirements for fire protection reasons. A typical area of application for G-glazing is the openings for lighting installed in corridor walls, which have to be constructed fire-retarding (F 30) as the side walls of escape routes. The lower edge of the glass must in this case be at least 1.80 m above floor level, so that in case of fire the corridor remains usable in the radiation shadow.

Construction
Classified materials for the construction of conventional massive load-bearing or non-load-bearing walls are shown in → 8. Steel columns and steel supporting beams are today normally fitted with box-shaped claddings of fire protection boards, whose thickness depends on the profile dimensions and the required fire resistance class → 1 – 3. There are also non-foaming coatings (to F 90) and composite constructions with concrete filling, if necessary with additional reinforcement (F 60). Non-load-bearing separating walls can be constructed as stud partitions of various qualities → 4 – 6.

Thermal bridge
Thermal bridges are parts of building elements with low thermal insulation compared with surrounding areas. This results in the proportion of the surface air film in the overall resistance increasing so that the surface temperature of the inner side of the thermal bridge sinks and condensation forms.

Good thermal insulation includes not only highly insulated building components, but also the appropriate connections between the building elements. question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In office planning, which grid module dimensions have proved successful in recent years for (a) single-room offices and (b) office types based on the combi principle?
source: The modular dimensions, which have proved successful in recent years, are 1.50 m for single-room offices and 1.35 m for office types based on the combi principle.
context: Grid module spacings define possible room sizes through the resulting spacing of columns and façades. The fitting out and façade grids must be the same in order to enable the partitions to connect to the windows. The structural grid can be offset against the fitting out grid. This reduces the problem of connecting the partitions to columns, but loses space in the rooms, which contain columns. Because of the different lifecycles of the building elements, an adaptable module dimension should be chosen. The modular dimensions, which have proved successful in recent years, are 1.50 m for single-room offices and 1.35 m for office types based on the combi principle.

Modular dimension 1.50 m
This is the economical module dimension for single-room offices consisting mainly of double workstations. Workstation depth 2.20 m (80 cm desk, 1 m movement area, 40 cm shelf behind). With 10 cm wall thickness, this gives 4.40 m clear room space.
The usual depth of buildings with central corridors is 12–13 m. This dimension is only of limited practicality for combi-offices.

– additional filing storage; two computer workstations with a depth of 0.90 m, as recommended by accident insurance companies; one drawing board or drawing machine and one desk; one desk and meeting table for four people. question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Approximately how many workstations does a group office have, and how many workstations characterise the large-scale open-plan office landscapes made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation?

The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department.
Large-scale office landscapes with 100 or more workstations are made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation
context:
Group office: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department. This arrangement is preferred above all for creative, design or coordination and development activities with high internal communication needs.
→ 2

Group office: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department. This arrangement is preferred above all for creative, design or coordination and development activities with high internal communication needs.

Open-plan office: A form of office developed in the 1960s and 1970s of the last century. Large-scale office landscapes with 100 or more workstations are made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation; they stand for free communication and openness. Economical cubic structures, however, have the disadvantage of high maintenance costs. This form is not very popular among users → 3.

Single-room offices are suitable for independent or concentrated work, as a single-person room or for a few people in very small groups who need to exchange information constantly. This arrangement has been common in Germany since World War II and still has its justification when the requirements of the workplace correspond (→ Gruner, Jahr; Steidle, Kissler; or → new offices for the Federal Environment Office, Dessau, Sauerbruch, Hutton) or in newbuild high-rise offices, where the structure of the building can be so decisive that it leads to the very standardised character of spatial and organisational working practices.

A more sensitive relationship to the direct working environment is closely linked to the predominant value orientation in the company. This is reflected in the attitude to the quality of the workplace (daylight, environmental context, energy consumption), and the activity (ecological viewpoints, material use, waste disposal). The workplace is an important place for social interaction among the users, which is increasing in relevance due to formalised work structures (IT, work organisation etc.). Increased mental and physical stress leads to a greater awareness of the working environment (sufficient space, some personal choice in furnishings, ventilation, lighting, sufficient protection from disruptions). 75% of daily work takes place at the 'close and extended workplace' → ②. Necessary work contacts and collectively used facilities are significant, thus the requirement for a mixed provision of single and group rooms, 'personal' and 'collective' workplaces → ③ – ④. In addition to the refurbishment of existing office space, new spatial concepts involving single and group rooms are starting to appear (Fuchs, Gottschalk, Henkel → refs).

answer.text: A

The main room in a restaurant is the dining room. Its furniture and fittings should be appropriate for the business. A number of additional tables or chairs should be available, so that table groupings are flexible. Provide special tables for regulars. Side rooms and conference rooms should always be flexibly furnished in order to permit variations. A food bar with fixed stools can be arranged for customers in a hurry.
